title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences
abstract: Introduces an algorithm that learns a reward function from human preferences between pairs of trajectory segments, then optimizes a policy against that learned reward. This is the foundational method later adapted as RLHF for language models.
findings: Learns reward functions from human comparisons of trajectory segments rather than hand-engineered rewards, optimized in an RL loop.
Successfully trains complex novel behaviors (e.g. Atari games, simulated robot locomotion/backflips) using feedback on under 1% of the agent's interactions.
Reduces the cost of human oversight enough to be applied to state-of-the-art RL systems.

title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
abstract: Proposes PPO, a family of policy-gradient methods that alternate between sampling data and optimizing a clipped surrogate objective with multiple epochs of minibatch updates. PPO became the default RL optimizer for RLHF.
findings: Clipped surrogate objective enables multiple epochs of minibatch updates per data sample, unlike vanilla policy gradient.
Retains benefits of Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) but is much simpler to implement, more general, and has better sample complexity.
Outperforms other online policy gradient methods across a benchmark of continuous control and Atari tasks.

title: BioBERT: a pre-trained biomedical language representation model for biomedical text mining
abstract: A domain-specific BERT model continually pretrained on large-scale biomedical corpora (PubMed abstracts and PMC full-text) to address word-distribution shift in biomedical text mining.
findings: Adapts BERT to biomedicine via continued pretraining on PubMed abstracts and PMC full-text articles
Addresses the word-distribution shift from general-domain to biomedical corpora that degrades vanilla NLP models
Established a widely-adopted baseline for biomedical NER, relation extraction, and QA

title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
authors: Colin Raffel, Noam Shazeer, Adam Roberts, et al.
abstract: Introduces T5 and the C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus) dataset; conducts a large systematic study of pretraining objectives, architectures, and unlabeled datasets, establishing C4's cleaning recipe as a web-data standard.
findings: Introduces the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus (C4), a cleaned Common Crawl two orders of magnitude larger than Wikipedia.
C4 cleaning involves deduplication, discarding incomplete sentences, and removing offensive or noisy content.
Systematically compares pretraining objectives, architectures, unlabeled datasets, and transfer approaches across dozens of tasks.
Reframes all NLP tasks as text-to-text, achieving SOTA on summarization, QA, and classification benchmarks.
C4 became a foundational baseline corpus and cleaning recipe for later web-data curation work.

title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
abstract: Studies empirical scaling laws for language model performance on the cross-entropy loss, showing loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and compute, spanning more than seven orders of magnitude.
findings: Trained over 200 transformer LMs spanning seven orders of magnitude in compute, four in non-embedding parameter count, and three in tokens
Test loss follows a power-law with model size (N), dataset size (D), and training compute (C)
Architectural details such as width or depth have minimal effects within a wide range
Larger models are significantly more sample-efficient; compute-optimal training implies training very large models on relatively modest data and stopping well before convergence

title: Domain-Specific Language Model Pretraining for Biomedical Natural Language Processing
venue: arXiv (ACM Transactions on Computing for Healthcare)
abstract: Introduces PubMedBERT and the BLURB benchmark, arguing that for domains with abundant text like biomedicine, pretraining from scratch beats continual pretraining of general-domain models.
findings: Pretraining from scratch on in-domain biomedical text yields substantial gains over continual pretraining of general-domain models
Produced new state-of-the-art results across a wide range of biomedical NLP tasks
Introduced the BLURB comprehensive biomedical NLP benchmark and leaderboard

title: What Disease does this Patient Have? A Large-scale Open Domain Question Answering Dataset from Medical Exams
abstract: Introduces MedQA, the first free-form multiple-choice OpenQA dataset built from professional medical board exams across English and Chinese, a foundational vertical benchmark.
findings: First free-form multiple-choice medical OpenQA dataset, with 12,723 English, 34,251 simplified Chinese, and 14,123 traditional Chinese questions
Drawn from US, mainland China, and Taiwan medical licensing examinations
At publication, best methods reached only 36.7% (English), 42.0% (traditional Chinese), and 70.1% (simplified Chinese) test accuracy

title: Scaling Laws for Autoregressive Generative Modeling
abstract: Identifies empirical cross-entropy scaling laws across generative image, video, multimodal image-text, and math problem-solving domains.
findings: Autoregressive Transformers smoothly improve in performance following a power-law-plus-constant scaling law across four domains
Optimal model size depends on the compute budget via a power-law, with exponents nearly universal across data domains
The constant term in the scaling law allows estimation of the entropy of the true data distribution / irreducible loss

title: The Pile: An 800GB Dataset of Diverse Text for Language Modeling
authors: Leo Gao, Stella Biderman, Sid Black, et al.
abstract: Introduces The Pile, an 825 GiB open language-modeling dataset assembled from 22 diverse high-quality subsets, motivated by the finding that training-data diversity improves cross-domain generalization.
findings: An 825 GiB dataset constructed from 22 smaller high-quality subsets, many from academic or professional sources.
Models trained on the Pile improve significantly over both Raw Common Crawl and CC-100 across all Pile components.
Increased training-data diversity improves general cross-domain knowledge and downstream generalization for large-scale LMs.
Released in jsonlines format compressed with zstandard; became a standard open pretraining corpus and a default mixture baseline (e.g., for DoReMi).

title: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding
abstract: Introduces MMLU, a multiple-choice test of multitask accuracy spanning 57 subjects from elementary mathematics to US history, law, and computer science, designed to measure world knowledge and problem-solving across academic and professional domains.
findings: Covers 57 tasks including elementary mathematics, US history, computer science, and law
Most models tested had near random-chance accuracy; the largest GPT-3 model improved over random chance by almost 20 percentage points on average
Models still had near-random accuracy on socially important subjects such as morality and law, and lagged expert-level accuracy on all 57 tasks

title: Scaling Laws for Transfer
abstract: Studies empirical scaling laws for transfer learning in an unsupervised fine-tuning setting, characterizing 'effective data transferred' as a power-law of parameters and fine-tuning dataset size.
findings: Effective data transferred is well-described in the low-data regime by a power-law of parameter count and fine-tuning dataset size
Pre-training effectively multiplies the fine-tuning dataset size
Transfer, like overall performance, scales predictably in terms of parameters, data, and compute

title: Explaining Neural Scaling Laws
abstract: Proposes a theory explaining and connecting power-law scaling with dataset size and parameter count, identifying four distinct scaling regimes.
findings: Identifies variance-limited and resolution-limited scaling for both dataset and model size, for four total scaling regimes
Variance-limited scaling follows from the existence of a well-behaved infinite-data or infinite-width limit
Resolution-limited scaling is explained by models effectively resolving a smooth data manifold; exponents relate to data manifold dimension

title: Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset
abstract: Introduces MATH, a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems, each with a full step-by-step solution that can be used to teach models to generate derivations and explanations.
findings: Contains 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems with full step-by-step solutions
Accuracy remained relatively low even with enormous Transformer models
Argues that simply increasing budgets and parameter counts is impractical for strong mathematical reasoning if scaling trends continue

title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
abstract: Introduces Codex, a GPT model fine-tuned on GitHub code, and the HumanEval benchmark of 164 hand-written programming problems for measuring functional correctness of code synthesis from docstrings.
findings: HumanEval contains 164 original Python programming problems written to reduce data contamination
Codex solves 28.8% of HumanEval problems, while GPT-3 solves 0% and GPT-J solves 11.4%
Repeated sampling solves 70.2% of problems with 100 samples per problem

title: Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
abstract: Introduces GSM8K, a dataset of 8.5K high-quality, linguistically diverse grade-school math word problems, and proposes training verifiers to rank model completions for improved multi-step reasoning.
findings: GSM8K contains 8.5K high-quality, linguistically diverse grade-school math word problems
Verification significantly improves performance on GSM8K versus finetuning alone
Verification scales more effectively with increased data than the finetuning baseline

title: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold
abstract: DeepMind's AlphaFold2, a neural network trained on experimentally-resolved protein structures, achieved near-experimental accuracy at the CASP14 assessment, a landmark data-driven moat in structural biology.
findings: Outperformed all other approaches at the CASP14 assessment by a wide margin
On average the fraction of a protein structure correctly predicted crossed the 90% mark (high GDT accuracy)
Success attributed to a novel neural architecture trained on available 3D experimentally-resolved protein structures

title: Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better
authors: Katherine Lee, Daphne Ippolito, Andrew Nystrom, et al. (incl. Nicholas Carlini)
abstract: Shows that standard LM datasets contain many near-duplicates and long repeated substrings, and that deduplicating them reduces memorization, improves training efficiency, and corrects train-test overlap.
findings: Existing datasets contain many near-duplicate examples; over 1% of unprompted model output is copied verbatim from training data.
C4 contains a single 61-word English sentence repeated over 60,000 times, removed via their two deduplication tools.
Deduplication makes models emit memorized text ten times less frequently.
Deduplicated models require fewer training steps to reach the same or better accuracy.
Train-test overlap affects over 4% of the validation set of standard datasets, so dedup enables more accurate evaluation.

title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
abstract: The InstructGPT paper: fine-tunes GPT-3 with supervised demonstrations then RLHF on ranked outputs to align models with user intent. Establishes the canonical SFT -> reward model -> PPO RLHF pipeline.
findings: Outputs from the 1.3B InstructGPT model are preferred to outputs from the 175B GPT-3, despite 100x fewer parameters.
InstructGPT shows improvements in truthfulness and reductions in toxic output generation with minimal regressions on public NLP datasets.
Three-stage recipe: supervised fine-tuning on labeler demonstrations, reward model trained on output rankings, then PPO against the reward model.

title: STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning
abstract: A self-improvement loop where a model generates chain-of-thought rationales, keeps those that yield correct answers, rationalizes wrong ones given the correct answer, finetunes on successful rationales, and repeats.
findings: Iteratively bootstraps reasoning from a small number of rationale examples plus a large dataset without rationales
Significantly outperforms a model finetuned to directly predict final answers across multiple datasets
Performs comparably to finetuning a 30x larger model on CommonsenseQA

title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
abstract: The Chinchilla paper shows existing large LMs are significantly undertrained, and that model size and training tokens should be scaled equally for compute-optimal training.
findings: Trained over 400 models from 70M to over 16B parameters on 5 to 500B tokens
For compute-optimal training, model size and number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size, training tokens should also double
Chinchilla (70B, 4x more data) uses the same compute as Gopher (280B) but outperforms Gopher, GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B), and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B)
Chinchilla reaches state-of-the-art average accuracy of 67.5% on MMLU, a >7% improvement over Gopher

title: Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
abstract: Applies preference modeling and RLHF to fine-tune LLMs into helpful and harmless assistants, and releases the HH-RLHF preference dataset. Studies online iterated RLHF training.
findings: Alignment training improves performance on almost all NLP evaluations and is compatible with training for specialized skills like python coding and summarization.
Iterated online RLHF updates preference models and RL policies on a weekly cadence with fresh human feedback, efficiently improving datasets and models.
Identifies a roughly linear relation between the RL reward and the square root of the KL divergence between the policy and its initialization.

title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
abstract: Studies how repeated data harms language model training, finding a double-descent degradation regime and using interpretability to explain the mechanism.
findings: Found a strong double-descent phenomenon where repeated data can cause test loss to increase midway through training
A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe performance degradation
Data repetition disproportionately damages copying and induction heads, shifting models from generalization toward memorization

title: Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and extrapolating the capabilities of language models
abstract: Introduces BIG-bench, a massive collaborative benchmark of 204 diverse tasks intended to probe and extrapolate the capabilities of large language models beyond existing evaluations.
findings: Consists of 204 tasks contributed by 450 authors across 132 institutions
Task topics span linguistics, childhood development, math, common-sense reasoning, biology, physics, social bias, and software development
Focuses on tasks believed to be beyond the capabilities of current language models

title: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models
abstract: Defines emergent abilities as those not present in smaller models but present in larger models, arguing they cannot be predicted by extrapolating smaller-model performance.
findings: An ability is 'emergent' if not present in smaller models but present in larger models
Certain capabilities (e.g., multi-step reasoning) only manifest above certain scale thresholds
Emergent abilities appear as sharp, unpredictable transitions when plotted against scale

title: Beyond neural scaling laws: beating power law scaling via data pruning
abstract: Shows that error-vs-dataset-size power-law scaling can be broken and reduced toward exponential scaling given a high-quality data pruning metric.
findings: In theory and practice, good data pruning can beat power-law scaling, approaching exponential scaling of error with pruned dataset size
Demonstrated better-than-power-law scaling on ResNets trained on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and ImageNet
Performed the first large-scale benchmarking study of ten different data pruning metrics on ImageNet

title: Solving Quantitative Reasoning Problems with Language Models
abstract: Introduces Minerva, a PaLM-based model further trained on a curated technical corpus of arXiv papers and math-typeset web pages, achieving state-of-the-art quantitative reasoning.
findings: Built on PaLM with further training on a 118GB dataset of arXiv scientific papers and web pages with LaTeX/MathJax math content
Achieves state-of-the-art on technical benchmarks without external tools
Correctly answers nearly a third of 200+ undergraduate-level STEM problems requiring quantitative reasoning

title: Challenging BIG-Bench Tasks and Whether Chain-of-Thought Can Solve Them
abstract: Introduces BIG-Bench Hard (BBH), a suite of 23 difficult BIG-Bench tasks where prior LM evaluations did not beat the average human rater, and studies the effect of chain-of-thought prompting.
findings: BBH is a suite of 23 challenging BIG-Bench tasks where prior LMs did not outperform the average human rater
Chain-of-thought prompting lets PaLM surpass average human-rater performance on 10 of 23 tasks
With CoT, Codex (code-davinci-002) surpasses average human-rater performance on 17 of 23 tasks
CoT enables emergent task performance on several BBH tasks with otherwise flat scaling curves

title: BioGPT: Generative Pre-trained Transformer for Biomedical Text Generation and Mining
abstract: A domain-specific generative Transformer pre-trained on 15M PubMed abstracts, optimized for biomedical generation tasks unlike BERT-based understanding models.
findings: Achieves 44.98%, 38.42%, and 40.76% F1 on BC5CDR, KD-DTI, and DDI end-to-end relation extraction tasks respectively
Reaches 78.2% accuracy on PubMedQA
Pre-trained on 15M PubMed abstracts with a Transformer decoder architecture, enabling generative tasks beyond BERT-style understanding

title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
authors: Leo Gao, John Schulman, Jacob Hilton
abstract: Studies reward hacking / Goodharting in RLHF using a synthetic setup where a fixed 'gold' reward model plays the role of humans, and fits scaling laws for how gold-reward score degrades as one over-optimizes a proxy reward model.
findings: Over-optimizing a proxy reward model against ground truth follows Goodhart's law: gold-reward score eventually drops as proxy score keeps rising.
Derives functional forms (scaling laws) relating gold reward to the KL distance of optimization, for both best-of-n sampling and RL.
The relationship depends on reward model parameter count and the size of the reward model training dataset.

title: Large Language Models Can Self-Improve
abstract: Shows an LLM can self-improve using only unlabeled data by generating high-confidence chain-of-thought answers via self-consistency and finetuning on its own self-generated solutions.
findings: Improves a 540B LLM on GSM8K 74.4%->82.1%, DROP 78.2%->83.0%, OpenBookQA 90.0%->94.4%, ANLI-A3 63.4%->67.9%
Achieves state-of-the-art-level performance without any ground-truth labels
Uses CoT prompting plus self-consistency to select high-confidence rationale-augmented answers as finetuning targets

title: Broken Neural Scaling Laws
abstract: Introduces a smoothly broken power law (BNSL) functional form that models and extrapolates scaling behavior, including non-monotonic and inflection-point behaviors, across many domains.
findings: The smoothly broken power law (BNSL) accurately models and extrapolates scaling as a function of compute, parameters, dataset size, or upstream performance
Yields considerably more accurate extrapolations than other functional forms
Can express behaviors other forms cannot, such as non-monotonic double-descent transitions and delayed, sharp inflection points (including 'emergent' jumps)

title: Will we run out of data? Limits of LLM scaling based on human-generated data
abstract: Forecasts demand for training data versus the stock of public human-generated text, estimating when LLM scaling will be constrained by data availability.
findings: If current trends continue, LMs will fully utilize the stock of human-generated public text between 2026 and 2032 (or slightly earlier if models are overtrained)
Stock of high-quality language data may be exhausted before 2026
Argues synthetic data generation, transfer learning from data-rich domains, and data-efficiency improvements might support further progress

title: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
abstract: HELM is a framework for transparent, reproducible LLM evaluation that measures multiple metrics across many scenarios, taxonomizing the space of use cases and metrics and benchmarking many models head-to-head.
findings: Measures 7 metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency) across 16 core scenarios
Evaluated 30 models from 12 organizations across 42 scenarios, with 12B tokens and 17M queries
Adopts a top-down approach, explicitly stating scenarios and metrics and articulating what current coverage misses

title: Solving math word problems with process- and outcome-based feedback
abstract: First comprehensive comparison of process-based vs outcome-based supervision on a natural-language reasoning task (GSM8K), examining whether supervising intermediate reasoning steps beats supervising only the final answer.
findings: On final-answer error rate, process- and outcome-based supervision achieve similar results on GSM8K.
Process-based feedback (or outcome-based feedback combined with a learned step-level reward model) is needed to substantially reduce reasoning trace errors.
Establishes the process-vs-outcome supervision framing later central to PRM work.

title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
abstract: Introduces Constitutional AI and RLAIF: trains a harmless assistant using a set of written principles (a 'constitution') so that AI-generated critiques and AI preference labels replace human harmlessness labels in the RL phase.
findings: Coined RLAIF (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback): the RL phase uses AI-generated preference labels for harmlessness instead of human labels.
Two stages: supervised self-critique/revision, then RL from AI feedback using a preference model over constitutional principles.
Produces models that are both harmless and non-evasive, engaging with harmful queries by explaining objections rather than refusing outright.

title: Unnatural Instructions: Tuning Language Models with (Almost) No Human Labor
abstract: Collects a large instruction-tuning dataset with almost no human labor by prompting a language model with three seed examples to elicit new instructions, then rephrasing them for expansion.
findings: Collected 64K examples from 3 seed examples, expanded to ~240K instruction-input-output examples via rephrasing
Despite noise, training on Unnatural Instructions rivals manually-curated open-source datasets
Surpasses T0++ and Tk-Instruct across various benchmarks

title: Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions
abstract: A framework that bootstraps instruction-tuning data from a model's own generations: the model produces instructions, inputs, and outputs, which are filtered and used to finetune the original model.
findings: Applied to vanilla GPT-3, yields a 33% absolute improvement over the original model on Super-NaturalInstructions
Resulting performance is on par with InstructGPT-001, which used private user data and human annotations
Generates ~52K instructions and ~82K input-output instances from only 175 seed tasks

title: Large Language Models Encode Clinical Knowledge
abstract: Introduces the MultiMedQA benchmark and Med-PaLM, using instruction prompt tuning to align Flan-PaLM to medicine, plus a human-evaluation framework across factuality, harm, and bias.
findings: Flan-PaLM achieved 67.6% accuracy on MedQA (US Medical License Exam), surpassing prior state-of-the-art by over 17%
Introduced MultiMedQA, combining six existing medical QA datasets plus the new HealthSearchQA free-response dataset
Proposed instruction prompt tuning to create Med-PaLM and a multi-axis human evaluation framework (factuality, precision, possible harm, bias)

title: Data Selection for Language Models via Importance Resampling
authors: Sang Michael Xie, Shibani Santurkar, Tengyu Ma, Percy Liang
abstract: Introduces DSIR, a scalable framework that estimates importance weights in a reduced n-gram feature space and selects pretraining data via importance resampling to match a desired target distribution.
findings: Formalizes data selection as choosing a subset of raw data to match a target distribution given unlabeled target samples.
Instantiated with hashed n-gram features, it selects 100M documents from the full Pile in 4.5 hours.
For domain-specific continued pretraining, DSIR performs comparably to expert curation across 8 target distributions.
For general-domain pretraining (target = Wikipedia and books), DSIR improves over baseline selection methods.
Extends classic low-dimensional importance resampling to tractable high-dimensional LM data selection.

title: SemDeDup: Data-efficient learning at web-scale through semantic deduplication
authors: Amro Abbas, Kushal Tirumala, Dániel Simig, Surya Ganguli, Ari S. Morcos
abstract: Proposes SemDeDup, which uses embeddings from pretrained models to identify and remove semantic duplicates (semantically similar but not identical pairs) that exact-match deduplication misses.
findings: Leverages pretrained-model embeddings to find semantic duplicates beyond exact-match dedup.
On a subset of LAION, removes 50% of the data with minimal performance loss, effectively halving training time.
Removing semantic duplicates preserves performance and speeds up learning.
Targets web-scale uncurated datasets (e.g., LAION) that contain large redundancy beyond exact duplicates.

title: BloombergGPT: A Large Language Model for Finance
abstract: A 50-billion-parameter LLM purpose-built for finance, trained on a massive proprietary financial corpus mixed with general-purpose data, the first reported finance-domain LLM.
findings: 50B-parameter model trained on a 363 billion token financial dataset augmented with 345 billion tokens of general-purpose data
Outperforms existing open models of similar size on financial tasks by large margins
Maintains on-par or better performance on general NLP benchmarks, showing domain specialization did not sacrifice general ability

title: WizardLM: Empowering Large Language Models to Follow Complex Instructions
abstract: Introduces Evol-Instruct, an evolutionary algorithm that uses LLMs to rewrite simple instructions into progressively more complex ones (in-depth and in-breadth evolving) to create diverse, difficult instruction-tuning data.
findings: In-depth Evolving uses five operations: add constraints, deepening, concretizing, increase reasoning steps, complicate input; In-breadth Evolving generates new instructions
Evol-Instruct data is rated superior to human-created instructions in human evaluations on a complexity-balanced testbed
WizardLM outputs are preferred over ChatGPT outputs on high-complexity instructions

title: Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?
abstract: Argues that apparent emergent abilities of LLMs are largely an artifact of the evaluation metric chosen rather than fundamental changes in model behavior with scale.
findings: Nonlinear or discontinuous metrics produce apparent emergent abilities; linear or continuous metrics yield smooth, predictable changes
Alleged emergent abilities evaporate with different metrics or with better statistics
Emergence may not be a fundamental property of scaling AI models
Claims emergent abilities appear due to the researcher's choice of metric rather than fundamental changes in model behavior with scale
Nonlinear or discontinuous metrics (e.g., exact-match accuracy) produce apparent emergence
Linear or continuous metrics produce smooth, continuous, predictable performance changes with scale

title: Distilling Step-by-Step! Outperforming Larger Language Models with Less Training Data and Smaller Model Sizes
abstract: Extracts natural-language rationales (intermediate reasoning steps) from LLMs and uses them as additional supervision in a multi-task framework to train small task-specific models more data-efficiently.
findings: A 770M T5 outperforms few-shot prompted 540B PaLM using only 80% of available examples, a >700x model-size reduction
On e-SNLI, a 220M T5 outperforms 540B PaLM
Outperforms both standard finetuning and standard distillation while using less training data

title: StarCoder: may the source be with you!
abstract: BigCode's open 15.5B-parameter code LLMs trained on The Stack, a large collection of permissively-licensed GitHub repositories with opt-out tooling.
findings: StarCoder/StarCoderBase are 15.5B-parameter models with 8K context, infilling, and multi-query attention for fast inference
StarCoderBase trained on 1 trillion tokens from The Stack (permissively licensed GitHub repos with an opt-out process)
StarCoder fine-tuned on 35B additional Python tokens specialized the model for Python

title: Towards Expert-Level Medical Question Answering with Large Language Models
abstract: Introduces Med-PaLM 2, combining PaLM 2 base improvements with medical domain fine-tuning and ensemble refinement prompting to reach near expert-level performance on medical QA benchmarks.
findings: Med-PaLM 2 scored up to 86.5% on MedQA (USMLE-style), improving over Med-PaLM by over 19% and setting a new state-of-the-art
Approached or exceeded state-of-the-art on MedMCQA, PubMedQA, and MMLU clinical-topic datasets
In pairwise ranking of 1066 consumer medical questions, physicians preferred Med-PaLM 2 answers over physician answers on eight of nine clinical-utility axes (p < 0.001)

title: DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining
authors: Sang Michael Xie, Hieu Pham, Xuanyi Dong, et al.
abstract: Proposes DoReMi (Domain Reweighting with Minimax Optimization), which trains a small proxy model with Group DRO over domains to produce domain weights that are then used to resample data for training a much larger model.
findings: Uses a 280M proxy model with Group DRO to set domain weights, then trains an 8B model (30x larger) more efficiently.
Improves average few-shot downstream accuracy by 6.5 percentage points over a baseline trained on The Pile's default domain weights.
Reaches the baseline accuracy with 2.6x fewer training steps.
On The Pile, dramatically upweights Pile-CC web text (0.112 to 0.606) while downweighting ArXiv (0.105 to 0.004), PubMed Central, and StackExchange.
Domain weights are produced without any knowledge of downstream tasks.

title: To Repeat or Not To Repeat: Insights from Scaling LLM under Token-Crisis
authors: Fuzhao Xue, Yao Fu, Wangchunshu Zhou, Zangwei Zheng, Yang You
abstract: Empirically investigates repeating pretraining data for additional epochs under a 'token crisis,' analyzing overfitting/multi-epoch degradation, its contributing factors, and mitigation via regularization and mixture-of-experts.
findings: Repeating data for more epochs makes models susceptible to overfitting, causing multi-epoch degradation.
Significant factors for degradation are dataset size, model parameters, and training objectives; dataset quality and model FLOPs are less influential.
Widely used regularization (e.g., dropout) can alleviate multi-epoch degradation.
Mixture-of-experts enables cost-effective hyperparameter tuning that transfers to compute-intensive dense LLMs.
Motivated by high-quality web text approaching its scaling limit for LLMs.

title: The False Promise of Imitating Proprietary LLMs
abstract: A critical analysis of finetuning weaker models on outputs from stronger proprietary models (e.g., ChatGPT), arguing that imitation closes little of the real capability gap and mainly mimics style.
findings: Imitation models initially appeared competitive with ChatGPT to crowd workers, but targeted automatic evaluations found they closed little to none of the capability gap on tasks not heavily supported in imitation data
Imitation models adopt the style of the teacher but not its factuality/reasoning, exposing a gap human raters miss
Argues the highest-leverage action is improving base models rather than imitation finetuning

title: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
authors: Niklas Muennighoff, Alexander M. Rush, et al.
abstract: Studies LLM scaling when data is limited, running experiments up to 900B tokens and 9B parameters to quantify how repeating data and adding compute affect loss, and fits a data-constrained scaling law generalizing Chinchilla.
findings: Experiments vary data repetition and compute up to 900B training tokens and 9B parameter models.
Up to 4 epochs of repeated data yields negligible changes to loss compared to having unique data.
With more repetition the value of adding compute eventually decays to zero; 16 epochs mark clear diminishing returns.
Proposes and validates a scaling law that accounts for the decreasing value of repeated tokens and excess parameters.
Generalizes the Chinchilla scaling law to the repeated-data regime.
Ran experiments up to 900B training tokens and 9B parameter models
Training with up to 4 epochs of repeated data yields negligible changes to loss compared to unique data
Beyond ~16 epochs, returns from adding compute eventually decay to zero (diminishing returns)
Proposes and validates a scaling law for compute optimality accounting for decreasing value of repeated tokens and excess parameters

title: The Curse of Recursion: Training on Generated Data Makes Models Forget
abstract: Identifies 'model collapse': when models are recursively trained on data generated by prior generations, the tails of the original distribution disappear and models degrade irreversibly. Demonstrated in VAEs, GMMs, and LLMs.
findings: Use of model-generated content in training causes irreversible defects where the tails of the original content distribution disappear ('model collapse')
As the proportion of model-generated data rises, models lose diversity and rare/unique elements vanish
Effect is universal across generative model families (VAEs, Gaussian Mixture Models, LLMs); provides toy analytical models

title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
abstract: Introduces DPO, which reparameterizes the RLHF reward so the optimal policy has a closed form, turning preference alignment into a simple classification loss without a separate reward model or RL sampling loop.
findings: Solves the standard RLHF objective with a simple binary cross-entropy classification loss, eliminating reward-model training and RL sampling.
Fine-tuning with DPO exceeds PPO-based RLHF at controlling sentiment of generations.
Matches or improves response quality in summarization and single-turn dialogue while being substantially simpler and more stable to train.

title: Let's Verify Step by Step
abstract: Compares process supervision (feedback on each reasoning step) vs outcome supervision for training reward models on math, and releases PRM800K, a dataset of 800K step-level human correctness labels on MATH solutions.
findings: The process-supervised reward model solves 78% of problems from a representative subset of the MATH test set.
Process supervision significantly outperforms outcome supervision and majority voting, with the gap widening as the number of sampled solutions N increases.
Releases PRM800K: 800,000 step-level human feedback labels used to train the best reward model; active learning improves the efficacy of process supervision.

title: The RefinedWeb Dataset for Falcon LLM: Outperforming Curated Corpora with Web Data, and Web Data Only
abstract: Shows that stringently filtered and deduplicated web data alone can yield models that match or outperform models trained on curated corpora; introduces the RefinedWeb dataset used for Falcon LLMs.
findings: Properly filtered and deduplicated web data alone produces models that significantly outperform models trained on The Pile.
Stringent filtering plus deduplication yields a ~5-trillion-token web-only dataset competitive with state of the art.
Challenges the assumption that curated, high-quality sources are necessary alongside web data.
Publicly releases a 500-billion-token extract of RefinedWeb plus 1.3B and 7.5B parameter models trained on it.

title: Orca: Progressive Learning from Complex Explanation Traces of GPT-4
abstract: A 13B model that learns to imitate the reasoning process of GPT-4 by training on rich signals including explanation traces and step-by-step thought processes, rather than just shallow imitation of output style.
findings: Orca-13B surpasses Vicuna-13B by more than 100% on complex zero-shot reasoning benchmarks like Big-Bench Hard (BBH)
Achieves 42% improvement over Vicuna-13B on AGIEval
Uses large-scale, diverse imitation data with explanation traces and teacher assistance from ChatGPT to avoid learning only style without reasoning

title: PIXIU: A Large Language Model, Instruction Data and Evaluation Benchmark for Finance
abstract: Provides the first open financial LLM (FinMA) fine-tuned on LLaMA, a large financial instruction dataset, and a holistic financial evaluation benchmark.
findings: Releases the first open financial instruction dataset with 136K data samples for fine-tuning
Introduces FinMA (the financial LLM) fine-tuned on LLaMA plus an evaluation benchmark of 5 tasks and 9 datasets
Provides a holistic suite (FIT instruction data + FinBen-style evaluation) to assess financial LLMs

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
abstract: Systematically studies using strong LLMs as judges to evaluate chat assistants on open-ended questions, analyzing biases and agreement with human preferences via MT-bench and Chatbot Arena.
findings: Identifies position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases plus limited reasoning ability in LLM judges
Shows strong LLM judges like GPT-4 can match human preferences, achieving over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans
Released 80 MT-bench questions, 3K expert votes, and 30K conversations with human preferences

title: FinGPT: Open-Source Financial Large Language Models
abstract: An open-source, data-centric financial LLM framework emphasizing automatic data curation pipelines and lightweight LoRA adaptation to democratize internet-scale financial data.
findings: Takes a data-centric approach with an automatic data curation pipeline to handle finance's high temporal sensitivity and low signal-to-noise ratio
Uses lightweight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to build financial LLMs cheaply
Positioned as an open-source alternative to proprietary BloombergGPT to democratize financial data access

title: WizardCoder: Empowering Code Large Language Models with Evol-Instruct
abstract: Adapts the Evol-Instruct method to the code domain (Code Evol-Instruct) to generate complex code instruction data, producing WizardCoder models that excel on code-generation benchmarks.
findings: Surpasses all open-source Code LLMs by a substantial margin on HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP, and DS-1000
Outperforms the largest closed LLMs (Anthropic's Claude, Google's Bard) on HumanEval and HumanEval+
WizardCoder-34B achieves HumanEval comparable to GPT-3.5 and surpasses it on HumanEval+

title: Textbooks Are All You Need
authors: Suriya Gunasekar, Yi Zhang, Jyoti Aneja, et al.
abstract: Introduces phi-1, a 1.3B-parameter code LLM trained on 'textbook-quality' data: 6B tokens of filtered web code plus ~1B tokens of synthetic GPT-3.5-generated textbooks and exercises, showing high-quality data dramatically reduces required scale.
findings: phi-1 is a 1.3B-parameter Transformer trained for 4 days on 8 A100s.
Uses 6B tokens of 'textbook quality' web-filtered data plus 1B tokens of GPT-3.5-synthesized textbooks and exercises.
Despite small scale, attains 50.6% pass@1 on HumanEval and 55.5% on MBPP.
Demonstrates high-quality/synthetic data can substitute for much larger raw-data and compute budgets.
Finetuned on 'textbook-exercise-like' data to further boost coding performance.
phi-1 (1.3B params) attains 50.6% pass@1 on HumanEval and 55.5% on MBPP despite tiny scale
Trained on only 6B tokens of filtered web 'CodeTextbook' data plus ~1B tokens of synthetic textbooks
Finetuned on a 180M-token synthetic 'CodeExercises' dataset; finetuning unlocked emergent capabilities beyond the exercises themselves

title: Self-Consuming Generative Models Go MAD
abstract: Analyzes autophagous ('self-consuming') training loops where models are repeatedly trained on synthetic data, defining Model Autophagy Disorder (MAD) and characterizing the quality-diversity tradeoff across generations.
findings: Defines Model Autophagy Disorder (MAD); appreciable MADness arises in just a few generations
Without sampling bias, MADness degrades both quality and diversity; with sampling bias, quality can be maintained but diversity degrades even faster
Demonstrated empirically with state-of-the-art generative image models across three families of autophagous loops

title: Scaling Relationship on Learning Mathematical Reasoning with Large Language Models
abstract: Studies how pre-training loss, supervised data amount, and augmented data influence math reasoning, and proposes Rejection sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT) to augment training with model-generated correct reasoning paths.
findings: Combining rejection samples from multiple models pushes LLaMA-7B to 49.3% on GSM8K, vs 35.9% for plain supervised finetuning
Finds a log-linear relation between supervised data amount and performance; better models improve less from more data
RFT brings more improvement for less-performant LLMs, and more distinct reasoning paths help more

title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
abstract: A multi-dimensional benchmark of 8 distinct interactive environments for assessing LLM-as-Agent reasoning and decision-making abilities, highlighting gaps between commercial and open-source models.
findings: Consists of 8 distinct interactive environments to assess LLM-as-Agent reasoning and decision-making
Reveals significant performance differences between top commercial LLMs and open-source models acting as agents
Identifies poor long-term reasoning, decision-making, and instruction-following as key bottlenecks for agents

title: Self-Alignment with Instruction Backtranslation
abstract: Builds high-quality instruction-following data by 'backtranslating': a seed model generates instruction prompts for unlabeled web documents (self-augmentation), then selects high-quality pairs (self-curation), iterating to improve.
findings: Two iterations of finetuning LLaMa yields a model that outperforms all other LLaMa-based models on the Alpaca leaderboard not relying on distillation data
Combines self-augmentation (generating instructions for web text) with self-curation (filtering high-quality pairs)
Demonstrates highly effective self-alignment without distilling from a stronger model

title: Reinforced Self-Training (ReST) for Language Modeling
abstract: A growing-batch RL algorithm that alternates a Grow step (sampling a dataset from the current policy) and an Improve step (offline RL/finetuning on filtered samples), reusing offline data for efficiency.
findings: Two nested loops: Grow (sample dataset from latest policy) and Improve (improve policy on the fixed dataset via offline RL)
More efficient than online RLHF because the training dataset is produced offline and reused
Substantially improves machine-translation quality in a compute- and sample-efficient manner

title: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models
abstract: An interdisciplinary benchmark of legal-expert-designed tasks measuring legal reasoning in LLMs, mapping legal frameworks to evaluation tasks.
findings: Consists of 162 tasks covering six different types of legal reasoning
Tasks were hand-crafted by legal professionals and gathered from 40 contributors
Maps popular legal-reasoning frameworks to tasks to create a common vocabulary for lawyers and LLM developers

title: D4: Improving LLM Pretraining via Document De-Duplication and Diversification
authors: Kushal Tirumala, Daniel Simig, Armen Aghajanyan, Ari S. Morcos
abstract: Introduces D4, which combines embedding-space document deduplication with diversification (selecting cluster centers) on top of MinHash-deduplicated data to speed up LLM pretraining and improve downstream accuracy.
findings: Careful selection via pretrained-model embeddings, on top of deduplicated data, gives ~20% training-efficiency gains.
Improves average downstream accuracy on 16 NLP tasks by up to 2% at the 6.7B model scale.
Deduplicates and selects cluster centers in pretrained-model embedding space.
Repeating data intelligently consistently outperforms baseline training, while repeating random data performs worse than baseline.
Motivated by diminishing returns of simply scaling web data and the limits of simple MinHash dedup.

title: Code Llama: Open Foundation Models for Code
abstract: A family of code LLMs based on Llama 2 (7B-70B) with infilling, long-context support, and instruction-following, achieving state-of-the-art among open code models.
findings: Reaches up to 67% on HumanEval and 65% on MBPP, state-of-the-art among open models
Code Llama - Python 7B outperforms Llama 2 70B on HumanEval and MBPP, showing the value of code-domain specialization
Models trained on 16k-token sequences with improvements on inputs up to 100k tokens; outperform all other public models on MultiPL-E

title: RLAIF vs. RLHF: Scaling Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with AI Feedback
abstract: A controlled comparison of RLAIF (reward model trained on off-the-shelf LLM preference labels) against RLHF across summarization, helpful dialogue, and harmless dialogue, plus a direct-RLAIF variant.
findings: RLAIF achieves comparable performance to RLHF across summarization, helpful dialogue, and harmless dialogue generation.
RLAIF can outperform a supervised fine-tuned baseline even when the AI labeler is the same size as the policy, or the exact same checkpoint as the initial policy.
Introduces direct-RLAIF (d-RLAIF), obtaining rewards directly from an off-the-shelf LLM during RL (skipping reward-model training), which beats canonical RLAIF.

title: When Less is More: Investigating Data Pruning for Pretraining LLMs at Scale
authors: Max Marion, Ahmet Üstün, Luiza Pozzobon, et al. (incl. Sara Hooker)
abstract: Compares scalable data-quality estimators (perplexity, Error L2-Norm, memorization) for pruning pretraining data at scale, finding that simple perplexity-based pruning outperforms more expensive scoring methods.
findings: Evaluates perplexity, Error L2-Norm (EL2N), and memorization as scalable data-quality estimators.
The simple perplexity technique outperforms the more computationally expensive scoring methods.
Improves over a no-pruning baseline while training on as little as 30% of the original dataset.
Demonstrates data pruning can both reduce data volume and improve quality at scale.

title: Textbooks Are All You Need II: phi-1.5 technical report
abstract: Extends the phi approach to natural language reasoning, training phi-1.5 (1.3B params) primarily on curated 'textbook-quality' synthetic data, achieving performance comparable to models 5x larger on common-sense reasoning.
findings: phi-1.5 (1.3B params) performs comparably to models 5x larger on natural-language and reasoning tasks
Trained on phi-1's 7B tokens plus ~20B tokens of newly created synthetic 'textbook-like' data
Demonstrates synthetic data can instill reasoning while reducing toxic/biased content relative to web data

title: MetaMath: Bootstrap Your Own Mathematical Questions for Large Language Models
abstract: Bootstraps a math instruction dataset (MetaMathQA) by rewriting existing questions from multiple perspectives (forward/backward reasoning, rephrasing) without extra knowledge, then finetunes LLaMA-2 on it.
findings: MetaMath-7B achieves 66.4% on GSM8K and 19.4% on MATH, exceeding same-size SOTA by 11.5% and 8.7%
MetaMath-70B reaches 82.3% on GSM8K, slightly better than GPT-3.5-Turbo
Question bootstrapping (rephrasing, self-verification, FOBAR) augments data without new knowledge

title: OpenWebMath: An Open Dataset of High-Quality Mathematical Web Text
abstract: An open dataset of 14.7B tokens of mathematical web text extracted and filtered from Common Crawl, built to improve LLM reasoning via high-quality math pretraining data.
findings: Contains 14.7B tokens of mathematical webpages, filtered from over 200B HTML files down to 6.3 million documents
Spans over 130k different domains including forums, educational pages, and blogs
Includes a pipeline for extracting LaTeX/text and removing boilerplate, with quality filtering and deduplication

title: Llemma: An Open Language Model For Mathematics
abstract: Open math LLMs (7B/34B) created by continued pretraining of Code Llama on Proof-Pile-2, a mixture of scientific papers, math web data, and mathematical code.
findings: Continues pretraining Code Llama on Proof-Pile-2 (arXiv, web math data, and code totaling 55 billion unique tokens)
Outperforms all known open base models on the MATH benchmark and the unreleased Minerva suite on an equi-parameter basis
Capable of tool use and formal theorem proving without further finetuning; all artifacts openly released

title: GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark
abstract: A dataset of 448 expert-written multiple-choice questions in biology, physics, and chemistry that are extremely difficult and 'Google-proof,' designed for scalable oversight research on superhuman-knowledge models.
findings: 448 multiple-choice questions written by domain experts in biology, physics, and chemistry
PhD-level domain experts reach 65% accuracy (74% discounting clear mistakes identified in retrospect)
Skilled non-expert validators reach only 34% accuracy despite 30+ minutes with unrestricted web access
Strongest GPT-4-based baseline achieved 39% accuracy

title: GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants
abstract: GAIA proposes real-world questions requiring reasoning, multi-modality, web browsing, and tool use that are conceptually simple for humans but hard for advanced AI assistants.
findings: Consists of 466 questions requiring multiple reasoning steps, tool use, and often multi-modal input
Human respondents obtain 92% versus 15% for GPT-4 equipped with plugins
Departs from the trend of ever-harder-for-humans tasks, instead targeting human-easy questions that stress AI robustness

title: MEDITRON-70B: Scaling Medical Pretraining for Large Language Models
abstract: Open-source 7B and 70B medical LLMs built on Llama-2 with continued pretraining on a curated medical corpus of PubMed articles, abstracts, and clinical guidelines.
findings: MEDITRON-70B outperforms GPT-3.5 and Med-PaLM, and is within 5% of GPT-4 and 10% of Med-PaLM-2 on major medical benchmarks
Continued pretraining on a curated medical corpus (PubMed articles/abstracts plus internationally-recognized clinical guidelines)
Demonstrates significant gains over state-of-the-art baselines both before and after task-specific finetuning

title: Beyond Human Data: Scaling Self-Training for Problem-Solving with Language Models
abstract: Introduces ReST^EM, an expectation-maximization-based self-training method that generates samples, filters them with binary (correctness) feedback, finetunes on the survivors, and repeats, surpassing finetuning on human data.
findings: On MATH reasoning and APPS coding with PaLM-2, ReST^EM scales favorably with model size and significantly surpasses finetuning only on human data
Uses binary scalar feedback (e.g., answer correctness) to filter self-generated samples
Demonstrates models can go 'beyond human data' on verifiable tasks

title: Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations
abstract: Builds a process reward model (Math-Shepherd) trained on automatically constructed step-level supervision (no human annotation), used both for verification reranking and step-by-step PPO reinforcement.
findings: Automatically constructs process-wise supervision via completion-based estimation, removing reliance on manual step labels.
Step-by-step PPO with Math-Shepherd improves Mistral-7B from 77.9% -> 84.1% on GSM8K and 28.6% -> 33.0% on MATH.
Adding Math-Shepherd verification further raises accuracy to 89.1% (GSM8K) and 43.5% (MATH).

title: Evolutionary-scale prediction of atomic-level protein structure with a language model
abstract: Trains protein language models (ESM-2) up to 15B parameters on protein sequences; structural information emerges with scale, enabling fast single-sequence structure prediction via ESMFold.
findings: Trained transformer protein language models with up to 15 billion parameters; atomic-level structural information emerged as the model scaled
ESMFold is nearly as accurate as alignment-based methods (e.g. AlphaFold2) but considerably faster, using single sequences without MSAs
The increased speed enabled the ESM Metagenomic Atlas, containing more than 600 million metagenomic protein structures

title: Time Travel in LLMs: Tracing Data Contamination in Large Language Models
abstract: Proposes a method using 'guided instruction' prompts (with dataset name, partition, and a reference snippet) to detect data contamination in LLMs at both the instance and partition levels.
findings: Uses guided instruction prompting to elicit and detect memorized benchmark instances
Best method achieves 92% to 100% accuracy in detecting contamination across seven datasets versus human-expert evaluation
Finds GPT-4 is contaminated with the AG News, WNLI, and XSum datasets

title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
abstract: Introduces SWE-bench, an evaluation framework of real GitHub issues and corresponding pull requests across popular Python repositories, where models must edit a codebase to resolve an issue, verified by tests.
findings: Consists of 2,294 software engineering problems drawn from real GitHub issues and pull requests across 12 popular Python repositories
Resolving issues frequently requires coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes, and files and processing very long contexts
Best system (Claude 2) resolves only 1.96% of issues, showing the task is far from solved

title: Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws
abstract: Modifies Chinchilla scaling laws to account for inference cost, computing the optimal parameter count and training data size to train and deploy a model of given quality and inference demand.
findings: LLM developers expecting large inference demand (~1B requests) should train models smaller and longer than Chinchilla-optimal
Trained 47 models to validate the formula
Model quality continues to improve as tokens-per-parameter is scaled to extreme ranges (up to 10,000 tokens per parameter)

title: Self-Rewarding Language Models
abstract: The model acts as its own reward via LLM-as-a-Judge prompting, generating and scoring its own responses to build preference data for Iterative DPO, removing the bottleneck of a frozen external reward model.
findings: Finetuning Llama 2 70B over three iterations outperforms many existing systems on AlpacaEval 2.0, including Claude 2, Gemini Pro, and GPT-4 0613
During Iterative DPO, both instruction-following and the model's own reward-modeling ability improve together
Avoids the human-performance bottleneck of reward models trained on fixed human preferences
During Iterative DPO training, both instruction-following ability and the model's ability to give itself high-quality rewards improve simultaneously.
Aims to break the bottleneck of frozen, human-level reward models that cannot improve during training.
A Llama 2 70B fine-tuned over three iterations of self-rewarding outperforms several existing systems on the AlpacaEval 2.0 leaderboard.

title: DeepSeek-Coder: When the Large Language Model Meets Programming -- The Rise of Code Intelligence
abstract: Open code models (1.3B-33B) trained from scratch on 2 trillion tokens of a project-level code corpus with a fill-in-the-blank objective and 16K window.
findings: Trained from scratch on 2 trillion tokens (87% source code, 10% English code-related NL, 3% Chinese NL)
Achieves state-of-the-art among open-source code models and surpasses closed models like Codex and GPT-3.5
Uses project-level code corpus plus a 16K-window fill-in-the-blank task to enhance generation and infilling

title: Rephrasing the Web: A Recipe for Compute and Data-Efficient Language Modeling
abstract: Introduces WRAP (Web Rephrase Augmented Pre-training): an instruction-tuned model paraphrases web documents into styles like 'Wikipedia' or 'question-answer', and LLMs are jointly pre-trained on real plus synthetic rephrases.
findings: WRAP on C4 speeds up pre-training by ~3x
Improves perplexity by more than 10% on average across subsets of the Pile, and improves zero-shot QA accuracy across 13 tasks by more than 2%
Combines real and synthetic rephrased data rather than replacing real data, mitigating distribution shift

title: Dolma: an Open Corpus of Three Trillion Tokens for Language Model Pretraining Research
abstract: Releases Dolma, a 3-trillion-token open English corpus (used to train OLMo) built from web, scientific papers, code, books, social media, and encyclopedic content, plus an open curation toolkit and ablation-driven design.
findings: Three-trillion-token corpus sampled from a diverse set of domains, curated from ~200TB of raw text down to an 11TB dataset.
Built explicitly to enable open scientific study of how training-data choices affect model capabilities.
Provides an open data-curation toolkit (filtering, deduplication, mixing) alongside the corpus.
Serves as the pretraining corpus for the OLMo open language model from AI2.
Released openly on the HuggingFace Hub to improve transparency of pretraining data.

title: KTO: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization
abstract: Frames alignment objectives as 'human-aware losses' (HALOs) grounded in Kahneman-Tversky prospect theory, and introduces KTO, which maximizes utility from a binary desirable/undesirable signal rather than pairwise preferences.
findings: Argues part of DPO's success over cross-entropy comes from implicitly encoding human cognitive biases (a family of losses called HALOs).
KTO matches or exceeds preference-based methods (e.g. DPO) at scales from 1B to 30B despite learning only from a binary desirable/undesirable label.
Removes the need for paired preference data, since KTO works with unpaired good/bad examples.

title: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models
abstract: Introduces DeepSeekMath and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a PPO variant that drops the critic and estimates advantages from group-relative scores of multiple sampled responses, enabling efficient RL for math reasoning.
findings: Introduces GRPO, which foregoes a separate value/critic model and computes advantages from group-relative rewards of sampled outputs, cutting RL memory/compute.
DeepSeekMath-7B reaches 51.7% on the competition-level MATH benchmark without external toolkits or voting, approaching Gemini-Ultra and GPT-4.
GRPO later became the core RL algorithm behind DeepSeek-R1-style reasoning training.
DeepSeekMath 7B scores 51.7% on the competition-level MATH benchmark without external tools, approaching Gemini-Ultra and GPT-4; self-consistency over 64 samples reaches 60.9%
Continued pretraining on 120B math-related tokens sourced from Common Crawl via an iterative extraction pipeline
Introduces Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a memory-efficient PPO variant that drops the critic model

title: Scaling Laws for Downstream Task Performance of Large Language Models
abstract: Studies scaling of downstream task performance (machine translation) as a function of pretraining data size and the distribution alignment between pretraining and downstream data.
findings: With sufficient distribution alignment, both downstream cross-entropy and translation metrics (BLEU, COMET) improve monotonically with more pretraining data
Downstream BLEU can be predicted accurately with a log-law given good alignment
Under moderate misalignment, BLEU can fluctuate or worsen with more pretraining even as downstream cross-entropy monotonically improves

title: QuRating: Selecting High-Quality Data for Training Language Models
authors: Alexander Wettig, Aatmik Gupta, Saumya Malik, Danqi Chen
abstract: Captures human intuitions about data quality along four axes via LLM pairwise judgments, trains a QuRater model to score a 260B-token corpus, and studies how selecting on each quality criterion affects 1.3B-model training.
findings: Investigates four qualities: writing style, required expertise, facts & trivia, and educational value.
LLMs discern these qualities best when making pairwise judgments of texts.
Trains a QuRater model from pairwise judgments and annotates a 260B-token corpus with scalar ratings.
Selects 30B tokens per criterion and trains 1.3B-parameter models to compare the criteria.
Finds selecting on educational value and required expertise yields strong downstream performance.

title: A Survey on Data Selection for Language Models
authors: Alon Albalak, Yanai Elazar, Sang Michael Xie, et al.
abstract: A comprehensive survey of data-selection methods for language models, covering filtering, deduplication, mixing, and selection across pretraining and other training stages, with a unified taxonomy and open resources.
findings: Reviews data-selection methods spanning filtering, deduplication, and mixture optimization for LMs.
Argues naively training on all available data is neither optimal nor feasible given variable text quality.
Notes data selection can reduce the carbon footprint and financial cost of training by reducing required compute.
Frames data selection as deciding which candidate points to include and how to sample from them.
Accompanied by a public GitHub repository of resources (github.com/alon-albalak/data-selection-survey).

title: SaulLM-7B: A pioneering Large Language Model for Law
abstract: The first LLM designed explicitly for legal text, built on Mistral 7B and pretrained on a large English legal corpus, with a legal instruction fine-tuning method.
findings: First LLM designed explicitly for legal text comprehension and generation, built on the Mistral 7B architecture
Trained on an English legal corpus of over 30 billion tokens
Introduces a novel instructional fine-tuning method leveraging legal datasets; released under the MIT License

title: Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference
abstract: Describes Chatbot Arena, an open live platform that ranks LLMs via crowdsourced pairwise human preference votes, along with the statistical methods used for efficient and reliable ranking.
findings: Uses a pairwise comparison approach with crowdsourced votes from a diverse user base
Amassed over 240K votes over several months at the time of writing
Develops efficient sampling and statistical (Elo/Bradley-Terry) methods to rank models accurately and reliably

title: Unraveling the Mystery of Scaling Laws: Part I
abstract: Provides a transparent, step-by-step recipe to estimate the constant terms in scaling-law formulas from small models and predict attributes of much larger models before training.
findings: Estimates all constant terms in scaling-law formulas by training only on models with 1M~60M parameters
Accurately predicts attributes for models up to 33B parameters before training, including minimum test loss, minimum required training steps, critical batch size, and the full test-loss trajectory
Confirms power-law correlation between loss and model size, dataset size, and compute

title: LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code
abstract: A contamination-free code benchmark that continuously collects new competition problems over time from LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces, evaluating broader capabilities than just code generation.
findings: Continuously collects new problems over time from LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces to avoid contamination
Hosts 400 high-quality coding problems published between May 2023 and May 2024 (at release)
Evaluates self-repair, code execution, and test output prediction beyond generation; evaluated 18 base and 34 instruction-tuned LLMs

title: RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Language Modeling
abstract: The first dedicated benchmark and codebase for evaluating reward models, built from prompt-chosen-rejected trios spanning chat, reasoning, and safety, including pairs with subtle but verifiable reasons one answer should be preferred.
findings: Provides a structured benchmark of prompt-chosen-rejected trios across chat, reasoning, and safety categories to probe reward-model behavior.
Constructs comparison sets with subtle but verifiable reasons (e.g. bugs, incorrect facts) one response should be preferred.
Evaluates many reward models (classifier-based, DPO-derived, etc.) to surface their strengths, failure modes, and refusal behaviors.

title: Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance
authors: Jiasheng Ye, Peiju Liu, Tianxiang Sun, et al.
abstract: Discovers that model performance is a quantitatively predictable function of mixture proportions ('data mixing laws'), enabling prediction of unseen-mixture performance and selection of optimal mixtures from small-scale runs.
findings: Establishes function forms ('data mixing laws') making model performance predictable from mixture proportions.
Fitting these functions on sample mixtures reveals performance on unseen mixtures before running them.
Nests the laws of training steps, model sizes, and data mixing to predict large-model performance from small-scale training.
Guides selection of an ideal data mixture without exhaustive trial-and-error full runs.

title: Is Model Collapse Inevitable? Breaking the Curse of Recursion by Accumulating Real and Synthetic Data
abstract: Revisits model collapse under the realistic assumption that data accumulate rather than replace prior data, showing that accumulating synthetic data alongside the original real data avoids collapse.
findings: Replacing real data with synthetic data tends toward model collapse, confirming prior work
But accumulating successive generations of synthetic data alongside the original real data avoids model collapse
Demonstrated empirically by pretraining sequences of language models on text corpora, plus theoretical analysis

title: Scaling Laws for Data Filtering -- Data Curation cannot be Compute Agnostic
abstract: Shows that data filtering/curation decisions made independent of training compute are often suboptimal, and develops scaling laws relating data quality, repetition, and compute.
findings: Limited high-quality data rapidly loses utility when repeated, eventually requiring inclusion of unseen but lower-quality data
Optimal data curation depends on compute budget; the same filtering recipe is not optimal across compute scales
Scaling laws allow curating the best pool for top DataComp performance at various compute budgets, tracing a data-curation Pareto frontier

title: Best Practices and Lessons Learned on Synthetic Data for Language Models
abstract: A survey of synthetic data for LLMs covering applications (reasoning, tool use, alignment), generation and curation methods, evaluation, and open challenges including factuality, fidelity, and responsible use.
findings: Surveys synthetic data across pretraining, instruction tuning, reasoning, and alignment, consolidating best practices
Highlights key challenges: ensuring factuality/fidelity of synthetic data, avoiding amplification of biases, and preventing model collapse
Emphasizes responsible use and rigorous evaluation to build trustworthy models

title: Phi-3 Technical Report: A Highly Capable Language Model Locally on Your Phone
abstract: Introduces phi-3-mini, a 3.8B model trained on 3.3T tokens of heavily filtered web plus synthetic data, rivaling GPT-3.5 and Mixtral 8x7B while small enough to run on a phone.
findings: phi-3-mini (3.8B params, 3.3T tokens) achieves 69% on MMLU and 8.38 on MT-bench, rivaling Mixtral 8x7B and GPT-3.5
Innovation is entirely in the dataset: a scaled-up mix of heavily filtered web data and synthetic data
phi-3-small (7B) and phi-3-medium (14B) reach 75%/78% MMLU and 8.7/8.9 MT-bench

title: Observational Scaling Laws and the Predictability of Language Model Performance
abstract: Builds scaling laws from ~100 publicly available models rather than training new ones, showing performance lies on a low-dimensional capability space and that emergent phenomena are predictable.
findings: Uses ~100 publicly available models to build 'observational' scaling laws without training new models
LM performance is a function of a low-dimensional capability space; model families differ mainly in compute-to-capability efficiency
Several emergent phenomena follow smooth, sigmoidal behavior and are predictable from smaller/weaker models

title: SimPO: Simple Preference Optimization with a Reference-Free Reward
authors: Yu Meng, Mengzhou Xia, Danqi Chen
abstract: A simpler offline preference optimization algorithm that uses the average log-probability of a sequence as an implicit, reference-free reward and adds a target reward margin to the Bradley-Terry objective.
findings: Uses average log-probability as the implicit reward, eliminating the reference model required by DPO and better aligning the reward with generation.
Adds a target reward margin to encourage a larger gap between winning and losing responses.
The top SimPO model (built on Llama3-8B-Instruct) surpasses Claude 3 Opus on AlpacaEval 2 / Arena-Hard without substantially increasing response length.

title: MMLU-Pro: A More Robust and Challenging Multi-Task Language Understanding Benchmark
abstract: An enhanced version of MMLU that adds harder, reasoning-focused questions and expands the answer set from four to ten options, spanning 14 domains and over 12,000 questions to reduce saturation and guessing.
findings: Causes a significant accuracy drop of 16% to 33% compared to MMLU
Increases answer choices from four to ten and contains over 12,000 questions across 14 domains
Sensitivity to prompt variation decreased from 4-5% in MMLU to just 2% in MMLU-Pro across 24 prompt styles
Chain-of-Thought reasoning outperforms direct answering on MMLU-Pro, the opposite of the original MMLU

title: Benchmark Data Contamination of Large Language Models: A Survey
abstract: Surveys the problem of benchmark data contamination (BDC) in LLM evaluation, reviewing detection methods, its impacts, and alternative assessment approaches to mitigate associated risks.
findings: Provides a systematic review of benchmark data contamination (BDC) challenges in LLM evaluation
Categorizes detection methods and surveys risk-mitigation/alternative assessment strategies
Argues contamination inflates measured benchmark performance and undermines fair comparison

title: Magpie: Alignment Data Synthesis from Scratch by Prompting Aligned LLMs with Nothing
abstract: A self-synthesis method that extracts alignment data directly from aligned LLMs by inputting only the left-side chat template (up to the user-message position), prompting the model to auto-generate user queries and then responses.
findings: Aligned LLMs like Llama-3-Instruct generate user queries when given only the left-side template up to the reserved user-message position
Produces high-quality instruction data with no seed questions and no human labor
Models fine-tuned on Magpie data are competitive with models tuned on much larger supervised/official alignment datasets

title: DataComp-LM: In search of the next generation of training sets for language models
authors: Jeffrey Li, Alex Fang, Vaishaal Shankar, et al.
abstract: Introduces DCLM, a testbed and standardized 240T-token Common Crawl corpus for controlled data-curation experiments (filtering, dedup, mixing) at model scales from 412M to 7B parameters, with 53 downstream evaluations.
findings: Provides a standardized corpus of 240T tokens extracted from Common Crawl plus the OpenLM-based training framework and 53 downstream evaluations.
Model-based filtering is identified as the key lever for assembling a high-quality training set.
DCLM-Baseline trains a 7B model from scratch to 64% 5-shot accuracy on MMLU using 2.6T training tokens.
This is a 6.6 percentage-point MMLU improvement over the prior open-data SOTA (MAP-Neo) while using 40% less compute.
Participants compete on curation strategies at scales 412M-7B, making it a controlled benchmark for data-centric research.
Provides a standardized corpus of 240T tokens from Common Crawl, with model scales from 412M to 7B parameters and 53 downstream evaluations
Model-based filtering was key to assembling a high-quality training set
DCLM-Baseline trains a 7B model to 64% 5-shot MMLU accuracy with 2.6T tokens, a 6.6 percentage-point gain over MAP-Neo while using 40% less compute

title: The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale
abstract: Presents FineWeb, a 15-trillion-token English web corpus derived from 96 Common Crawl snapshots, with an extraction/filtering/deduplication pipeline validated through ablation studies, plus the educational subset FineWeb-Edu.
findings: 15-trillion-token dataset derived from 96 Common Crawl dumps (2013 to April 2024) that produces better-performing LLMs than other open pretraining datasets.
Pipeline uses language classification, URL filtering, C4-style and additional heuristic filters, and MinHash fuzzy deduplication, each validated via ablations.
FineWeb-Edu is a 1.3-trillion-token subset filtered for educational content using a quality classifier.
Models pretrained on FineWeb-Edu show dramatically better performance on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks like MMLU and ARC.
Releases the full dataset (44TB on disk) and the curation codebase for transparency.

title: LiveBench: A Challenging, Contamination-Free LLM Benchmark
abstract: A general-purpose benchmark designed to limit contamination by releasing frequently-updated questions from recent sources and scoring answers automatically against objective ground-truth values.
findings: First benchmark to combine frequently-updated questions from recent sources, automatic objective ground-truth scoring, and a wide variety of challenging tasks
Spans math, coding, reasoning, language, instruction following, and data analysis
Releases new questions monthly using recent arXiv papers, news articles, and IMDb synopses to limit contamination

title: RegMix: Data Mixture as Regression for Language Model Pre-training
authors: Qian Liu, Xiaosen Zheng, Niklas Muennighoff, et al.
abstract: Formulates data-mixture selection as a regression problem: train many tiny models on diverse mixtures, fit a regressor to predict performance of unseen mixtures, then apply the best predicted mixture to a large-scale run.
findings: Trains 512 1M-parameter models on 1B tokens to fit the regression and predict the best mixture, then trains a 1B model on 25B tokens.
The predicted mixture's 1B model performed best among 64 candidate 1B models with other mixtures.
Outperforms human selection up to 7B models on 100B tokens, matching or exceeding DoReMi with only 10% of the compute.
Predicts performance of held-out mixtures with 98.45% correlation.
Finds web corpora (Pile-CC), not nominally 'high-quality' data like Wikipedia, have the strongest positive correlation with downstream performance; single-task performance varies by up to 14.6%.

title: Scaling Parameter-Constrained Language Models with Quality Data
abstract: Extends scaling laws with a microscopic view of data quality via an 'effective training tokens' term combining text diversity and syntheticity.
findings: Introduces 'effective training tokens' as a function of text diversity and syntheticity (measured by a teacher model)
Pretrained over 200 models of 25M to 1.5B parameters on sampled synthetic data
Relates text quality, model size, training tokens, and accuracy across eight reasoning tasks, showing quality is critical for parameter-constrained models

title: Scaling Laws for Precision
abstract: Devises precision-aware scaling laws for training and inference, modeling how low-precision training and post-training quantization affect loss and effective parameter count.
findings: Training in lower precision reduces a model's 'effective parameter count', enabling prediction of additional loss from low-precision training
Degradation from post-training quantization increases as models are trained on more data, eventually making additional pretraining data actively harmful
Suggests training larger models in lower precision may be compute-optimal

title: FrontierMath: A Benchmark for Evaluating Advanced Mathematical Reasoning in AI
abstract: A benchmark of hundreds of original, exceptionally difficult unpublished mathematics problems spanning major branches of modern math, with automated verification to minimize contamination risk.
findings: Developed in collaboration with over 60 mathematicians, including IMO question writers and Fields medalists
Problems span computational number theory to abstract algebraic geometry and typically require hours or days for expert mathematicians to solve
Leading AI models solve less than 2% of FrontierMath problems despite near-perfect scores on GSM-8k and MATH

title: Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training
abstract: A fully open post-training recipe (data, code, weights) over SFT, DPO, and a new Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) stage, popularizing the RLVR term for skills with checkable answers.
findings: Introduces and names RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards), training on tasks with checkable answers like math and precise instruction-following.
Tulu 3 (on Llama 3.1 bases) surpasses the instruct versions of Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Mistral and even GPT-4o-mini and Claude 3.5-Haiku on its evaluation suite.
Releases full data, training code, recipes, and a decontaminated multi-task evaluation framework with held-out unseen evals.

title: Nemotron-CC: Transforming Common Crawl into a Refined Long-Horizon Pretraining Dataset
abstract: Presents methods for building a high-quality 6.3T-token pretraining dataset from Common Crawl that balances data quantity with accuracy, using classifier ensembling, synthetic data rephrasing, and reduced reliance on heuristic filters to retain far more unique tokens for long-horizon training.
findings: High-quality subset improves MMLU by 5.6 points over DCLM when training 8B models for 1T tokens.
Full 6.3T-token dataset matches DCLM on MMLU while containing four times more unique real tokens.
An 8B model trained for 15T tokens achieves +5 on MMLU versus Llama 3.1 8B.
Same model shows +3.1 on ARC-Challenge versus Llama 3.1 8B, and +0.5 average across ten diverse tasks.
