Combines classifier ensembling, synthetic rephrasing, and reduced heuristic filtering to retain more tokens.

title: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report
abstract: Technical report for DeepSeek-V3, a 671B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model (37B activated per token) using Multi-head Latent Attention and DeepSeekMoE, trained with an auxiliary-loss-free load-balancing strategy and FP8 training at scale.
findings: 671B total parameters with 37B activated per token; uses MLA for efficient inference and fine-grained DeepSeekMoE for cost-effective training.
Pioneers an auxiliary-loss-free load-balancing strategy and a multi-token prediction (MTP) training objective.
Trained on 14.8T tokens using FP8 mixed-precision training, with full training costing about 2.788M H800 GPU-hours.
Introduces DualPipe pipeline parallelism and optimized all-to-all communication to overlap computation and communication in MoE training.
Achieves performance competitive with leading closed models while remaining open-weight and compute-efficient.

title: AutoScale: Scale-Aware Data Mixing for Pre-Training LLMs
abstract: Shows that data mixtures performing well at small scales do not retain their advantage at larger scales, and proposes AutoScale, a two-stage scale-aware data composition framework that fits a parametric loss model at small budgets and extrapolates the optimal composition to larger budgets without further retraining.
findings: Achieves 28% faster perplexity reduction than baselines when pretraining GPT-2 Large.
Delivers up to a 38% speed-up over unweighted training.
Demonstrates that data mixtures optimal at small scales may not retain their advantage at larger scales.
Predicts optimal composition at large budgets via small-budget proxy fits, avoiding costly retraining, and achieves best-average results on downstream tasks.

title: Kimi k1.5: Scaling Reinforcement Learning with LLMs
abstract: Reports the RL training of Kimi k1.5, a multimodal reasoning LLM, emphasizing long-context scaling and a simplified RL framework that avoids MCTS, value functions, and process reward models.
findings: Achieves strong reasoning via long-context RL scaling without Monte Carlo tree search, value functions, or process reward models.
Reports state-of-the-art reasoning performance matching o1-level results on math/code/vision benchmarks (e.g. AIME, MATH-500, Codeforces).
Introduces effective long2short methods that transfer long-CoT reasoning gains into shorter-CoT models.

title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Shows reasoning can emerge from pure large-scale RL (DeepSeek-R1-Zero, no SFT cold start) and that a multi-stage cold-start + RL pipeline (DeepSeek-R1) reaches o1-level reasoning, with distilled smaller models released.
findings: DeepSeek-R1-Zero is trained via large-scale RL with no supervised fine-tuning, yet develops emergent self-reflection, verification, and strategy adaptation.
DeepSeek-R1 (multi-stage training with cold-start data before RL) achieves performance comparable to OpenAI-o1-1217 on reasoning tasks.
Open-sources R1-Zero, R1, and six dense distilled models (1.5B, 7B, 8B, 14B, 32B, 70B) based on Qwen and Llama.

title: Humanity's Last Exam
abstract: A multi-modal benchmark of expert-written questions at the frontier of human knowledge, created in response to MMLU-style saturation, with unambiguous, verifiable solutions that resist internet retrieval.
findings: Consists of 2,500 questions across dozens of subjects developed globally by subject-matter experts
Motivated by saturation: LLMs now exceed 90% accuracy on benchmarks like MMLU
State-of-the-art LLMs show low accuracy and poor calibration, with RMS calibration errors above 70% across all models

title: MedXpertQA: Benchmarking Expert-Level Medical Reasoning and Understanding
abstract: A challenging benchmark for expert-level medical knowledge and reasoning with both text and multimodal components, built through rigorous filtering, augmentation, and expert review, and including a reasoning-focused subset for advanced models.
findings: Contains 4,460 questions spanning 17 medical specialties and 11 body systems.
Includes Text and MM (multimodal) subsets; the MM subset uses expert-level exam questions with diverse images and rich clinical information.
Evaluates 18 leading models.
Designed to go beyond image-caption QA pairs of standard medical benchmarks, stressing multi-step clinical reasoning.

title: s1: Simple Test-Time Scaling
abstract: Demonstrates simple test-time scaling via a tiny curated SFT dataset plus 'budget forcing' to control inference-time compute, achieving strong reasoning with minimal data.
findings: Curates s1K, just 1,000 questions with reasoning traces selected for difficulty, diversity, and quality.
Introduces budget forcing: forcibly terminate thinking or extend it by appending 'Wait' to lengthen reasoning at test time.
After SFT on s1K, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (s1) exceeds o1-preview on competition math (MATH and AIME24) by up to 27%.
Budget forcing enables test-time scaling where extending thinking improves accuracy on AIME24.
Model, data, and code are fully open-sourced, showing strong reasoning is achievable with extremely small SFT data.

title: SmolLM2: When Smol Goes Big -- Data-Centric Training of a Small Language Model
abstract: Describes the data-centric training of SmolLM2, a 1.7B-parameter language model trained on ~11 trillion tokens through a multi-stage process that mixes web data with specialized datasets, introducing new curated datasets (FineMath, Stack-Edu, SmolTalk) to fill gaps in existing resources.
findings: SmolLM2 is a 1.7B-parameter model trained on approximately 11 trillion tokens.
Uses multi-stage training that interleaves web data with specialized datasets, refining mixtures based on performance.
Introduces three new curated datasets: FineMath, Stack-Edu, and SmolTalk.
Outperforms comparable small models including Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama3.2-1B.
Demonstrates that careful data curation and mixing can push small-model performance well beyond compute-matched baselines.

title: LIMO: Less is More for Reasoning
abstract: Challenges the assumption that complex reasoning requires massive training data, showing sophisticated math reasoning emerges from a few hundred high-quality SFT examples, and proposes the Less-Is-More Reasoning Hypothesis.
findings: LIMO achieves 63.3% accuracy on AIME24 and 95.6% on MATH500 using only ~800 curated training samples (~1% of data used by prior approaches).
Shows a 45.8% absolute improvement on out-of-distribution benchmarks, outperforming models trained on 100x more data.
Proposes the Less-Is-More Reasoning Hypothesis: when domain knowledge is encoded in pretraining, reasoning emerges from minimal, strategically designed demonstrations.
Uses multi-layer filtering (difficulty, knowledge-point diversity, reasoning-chain quality) to build the compact dataset.
Demonstrates strong data-efficiency and generalization for SFT-based reasoning.

title: Organize the Web: Constructing Domains Enhances Pre-Training Data Curation
authors: Alexander Wettig, Kyle Lo, et al.
abstract: Introduces WebOrganizer, which builds topic and format taxonomies for web pages and distills a large LLM classifier into small models to label documents, enabling domain-aware mixing as a complement to quality filtering.
findings: Develops two complementary domain taxonomies (topic and format), classifying web pages into 24 categories.
Scales labeling by distilling a Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct classifier into efficient 140M-parameter models.
Studies how to mix data from different domains to improve downstream tasks; combining effective topics and formats further boosts performance.
Constructing and mixing domains is a valuable complement to quality-based data curation.
Releases domain classifiers on HuggingFace and an interactive domain explorer.

title: Scaling Test-Time Compute Without Verification or RL is Suboptimal
abstract: Provides theory and experiments comparing verifier-free (distillation/cloning of search traces) versus verifier-based (RL, search against a verifier) methods for scaling test-time compute, showing the latter is provably better.
findings: Proves that verifier-based (VB) methods using RL or search against a verifier substantially outperform verifier-free (VF) approaches that distill/clone search traces, with the gap widening as test-time compute budget grows.
Shows a separation that scales with test-time budget, formalizing why verification matters for test-time scaling.
Empirically validates the gap on didactic and math reasoning settings (e.g., on a 3B/7B LLM), with VB outperforming VF by over 4x at large budgets in some settings.
Connects the advantage of verification to heterogeneity/anti-concentration of base policy correctness.
Argues compute should be invested in verifier-based RL rather than pure imitation when scaling inference.

title: Data-Efficient Pretraining with Group-Level Data Influence Modeling (Group-MATES)
abstract: Introduces Group-MATES, a method that optimizes pretraining data selection at the group level using a relational data influence model that captures relationships among training points, partitions data into clusters, and selects within clusters, evaluated under DataComp-LM setups.
findings: Achieves 3.5%-9.4% relative performance gains over random selection across 22 downstream tasks.
Nearly doubles the improvements achieved by state-of-the-art individual data selection baselines.
Reduces the number of tokens required to reach a given downstream performance by up to 1.75x.
Evaluated on DCLM 400M-4x, 1B-1x, and 3B-1x configurations using a relational (group-level) influence model.

title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
abstract: Fully open-sources a state-of-the-art large-scale RL system (algorithm, code, dataset) for long-CoT reasoning. Introduces the Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) algorithm with four key techniques to stabilize and improve RL.
findings: DAPO achieves 50 points on AIME 2024 with Qwen2.5-32B base, outperforming DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B (47 points) while using 50% of the training steps.

Introduces four techniques: Clip-Higher (prevents entropy collapse, boosts diversity), Dynamic Sampling (efficiency/stability), Token-Level Policy Gradient Loss, and Overlong Reward Shaping (reduces reward noise).
Fully open-sources training code (built on the verl framework) and a curated dataset for reproducibility.
Token-level loss is shown to be critical in long-CoT scenarios where response lengths vary widely.
Clip-Higher mitigates entropy collapse, maintaining exploration over training.

title: From 128K to 4M: Efficient Training of Ultra-Long Context Large Language Models
abstract: Presents a systematic recipe combining efficient continued pretraining and instruction tuning to extend LLM context windows from 128K up to 4M tokens while preserving general capabilities.
findings: Extends context length from 128K to 1M, 2M, and 4M tokens via efficient continued pretraining plus instruction tuning.
UltraLong-8B (built on Llama3.1-Instruct) achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse long-context benchmarks.
Models maintain competitive performance on standard short-context benchmarks, showing balanced extension.
Provides in-depth analysis of scaling strategies and data composition for long-context training.
Establishes a reproducible framework for efficiently scaling context length while preserving capabilities.

title: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
abstract: Critically re-examines whether RLVR enables LLMs to acquire reasoning abilities beyond their base models by measuring pass@k at large k across model families and benchmarks.
findings: RLVR-trained models outperform base models at small k (e.g., k=1) but base models achieve higher pass@k when k is large, indicating RL narrows rather than expands the reasoning boundary.
RL improves sampling efficiency toward already-reachable correct paths but does not elicit fundamentally new reasoning patterns beyond the base model's support.
Findings hold across multiple model families and reasoning benchmarks.
Distillation, by contrast, can genuinely introduce new knowledge/patterns unlike RLVR.
Suggests current RLVR is bounded by the base model's capability distribution.

title: The Leaderboard Illusion
abstract: Identifies systematic distortions in Chatbot Arena rankings arising from undisclosed private testing, selective score disclosure, sampling disparities, and data access asymmetries between providers.
findings: Identifies 27 private LLM variants tested by Meta in the lead-up to the Llama-4 release
Google and OpenAI received an estimated 19.2% and 20.4% of all arena data, while 83 open-weight models combined received only an estimated 29.7%
Access to Chatbot Arena data can yield relative performance gains of up to 112% on the arena distribution, indicating overfitting risk

title: Ultra-FineWeb: Efficient Data Filtering and Verification for High-Quality LLM Training Data
abstract: Tackles data-quality challenges via an efficient verification strategy and optimized seed-data selection, using a lightweight fastText-based classifier to filter high-quality content from FineWeb. Produces Ultra-FineWeb (~1T English tokens and 120B Chinese tokens) while reducing experimental and inference costs and improving classifier robustness.
findings: Releases Ultra-FineWeb with approximately 1 trillion English tokens and 120 billion Chinese tokens.
Uses a lightweight fastText-based classifier rather than heavier model-based scoring to cut inference cost.
Introduces an efficient verification strategy plus optimized seed-data selection to improve filter robustness.
Reports that LLMs trained on Ultra-FineWeb show significant improvements across multiple benchmark tasks versus FineWeb baselines.

title: AttentionInfluence: Adopting Attention Head Influence for Weak-to-Strong Pretraining Data Selection
abstract: Proposes a training-free pretraining data selection method that masks attention heads in a small model to score reasoning-intensive data, enabling weak-to-strong selection where a small model selects data to improve a much larger model, applied to the SmolLM corpus.
findings: Uses a 1.3B-parameter dense model as a training-free data selector via attention-head masking.
Selects 73B tokens from the 241B-token SmolLM corpus.
Pretrains a 7B-parameter model on 1T tokens using the selected data.
Yields improvements ranging from 1.4pp to 3.5pp across MMLU, MMLU-Pro, AGIEval-en, GSM8K, and HumanEval.
Demonstrates weak-to-strong generalization: a small selector improves a much larger trained model.

title: Qwen3 Technical Report
abstract: Technical report for Qwen3, a family of dense and MoE LLMs (0.6B-235B) that unifies thinking and non-thinking modes in a single model with a controllable thinking budget, trained via a multi-stage pipeline.
findings: Integrates thinking mode (multi-step reasoning) and non-thinking mode (rapid responses) into one model with dynamic mode switching.
Introduces a thinking-budget mechanism letting users allocate inference compute adaptively by specifying a token budget.
Flagship models follow a four-stage training pipeline, the first two stages building thinking ability (long-CoT cold start + reasoning RL).
Spans dense and MoE architectures from 0.6B to 235B parameters.
Uses strong-to-weak distillation to transfer thinking/non-thinking behavior to smaller models, reducing compute versus per-model RL.

title: LEXam: Benchmarking Legal Reasoning on 340 Law Exams
abstract: A legal reasoning benchmark derived from real law school exams in English and German, covering open-ended and multiple-choice formats, with an ensemble LLM-judge approach validated by human legal experts.
findings: Comprises 7,537 law exam questions drawn from 340 law exams across 116 law school courses.
Spans both English and German, in open-ended and multiple-choice formats.
Finds current LLMs notably struggle with open questions requiring structured, multi-step legal reasoning.
Effectively differentiates models with varying capability levels.

title: BizFinBench: A Business-Driven Real-World Financial Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs
abstract: A real-world financial benchmark of annotated Chinese queries spanning five dimensions (numerical calculation, reasoning, information extraction, prediction recognition, knowledge QA), evaluated with an IteraJudge protocol to reduce evaluator bias.
findings: Comprises 6,781 annotated queries across 9 fine-grained categories within 5 dimensions.
Evaluates 25 proprietary and open-source models; no model dominates across all tasks.
Numerical Calculation top scores: DeepSeek-R1 64.04, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 63.18; Reasoning: ChatGPT-o3 83.58, Gemini-2.0-Flash 81.15.
LLMs handle routine financial queries adequately but struggle with complex reasoning scenarios.

title: Toward Scientific Reasoning in LLMs: Training from Expert Discussions via Reinforcement Learning (Genome-Bench)
abstract: An end-to-end pipeline that converts over a decade of genome-engineering expert forum discussions into an RL-friendly multiple-choice benchmark (Genome-Bench), then fine-tunes LLMs with rule-based rewards to improve domain-specific scientific reasoning.
findings: Builds Genome-Bench with over 3,000 high-quality QA pairs from real-world expert discussions.
RL from scientific discussions improves model performance by more than 15% over the base model on Genome-Bench.
Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B reaches performance comparable to leading models such as DeepSeek-R1.
Described as the first end-to-end pipeline for teaching LLMs to reason from scientific discussions, with potential to generalize beyond biology.

title: SWE-rebench: An Automated Pipeline for Task Collection and Decontaminated Evaluation of Software Engineering Agents
abstract: An automated pipeline that continuously extracts real-world interactive software engineering tasks from GitHub repositories, producing both a large-scale RL training dataset and a continuously refreshed, contamination-free evaluation benchmark for SWE agents.
findings: Releases a public dataset of over 21,000 interactive Python-based SWE tasks suitable for RL of agents at scale.
Provides a continuously refreshed, contamination-free benchmark built from fresh GitHub tasks.
Comparison against SWE-bench Verified shows performance of some language models may be inflated due to data contamination.
Targets the twin problems of scarce real-environment training data and rapid benchmark obsolescence.

title: The Entropy Mechanism of Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Language Models
abstract: Studies the entropy collapse problem that limits scaling RL for reasoning LLMs, providing theoretical analysis of entropy dynamics and proposing techniques to maintain exploration.
findings: Identifies that tokens with strong positive covariance between probability and advantage primarily drive entropy collapse during RL.
Proposes Clip-Cov and KL-Cov, which clip or apply a KL penalty to high-covariance tokens to restrict their updates and preserve entropy.
These methods help the policy escape entropy collapse and achieve better downstream performance, enabling more sustained RL scaling.
Provides a predictable relationship (entropy-performance exchange) where policy entropy decays as performance rises, bottlenecking improvement.
Maintaining exploration directly translates into higher final reasoning accuracy.

title: ProRL: Prolonged Reinforcement Learning Expands Reasoning Boundaries in Large Language Models
abstract: Introduces ProRL, a prolonged RL training methodology with KL divergence control, reference policy resetting, and a diverse task suite, arguing that with enough training RL can expand reasoning boundaries beyond the base model.
findings: RL-trained models consistently outperform base models across pass@k evaluations, including cases where base models fail entirely regardless of number of attempts.
Prolonged RL uncovers novel reasoning strategies inaccessible to base models even under extensive sampling, contrasting with the pass@k narrowing claim.
Reasoning boundary improvements correlate strongly with base-model task competence and training duration.
Uses KL divergence control and reference policy resetting to enable stable, long-duration RL training.
Releases the Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-Qwen-1.5B model weights.

title: OpenThoughts: Data Recipes for Reasoning Models
abstract: A systematic study of data-curation recipes for distilling reasoning into models via SFT, culminating in the OpenThoughts3-1.2M dataset and the OpenThinker3-7B model.
findings: OpenThinker3-7B (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct fine-tuned on OpenThoughts3-1.2M) is state-of-the-art among open-data models at the 7B scale.
Outperforms the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B model by 12.4 points on average across 12 reasoning benchmarks.
Scales the Sky-T1/OpenThoughts pipeline with augmented question diversity and synthetic question generation strategies.
Conducts over a thousand controlled experiments to identify effective data-curation choices (question sourcing, filtering, teacher selection).
Demonstrates that careful SFT distillation data design rivals or beats RL-trained reasoning at small scale.

title: The Common Pile v0.1: An 8TB Dataset of Public Domain and Openly Licensed Text
abstract: Addresses concerns about unlicensed text in LLM training by collecting, curating, and releasing an 8TB collection of openly licensed and public-domain text drawn from 30 diverse sources spanning research papers, code, books, encyclopedias, educational materials, and audio transcripts. The dataset is validated by training two 7B-parameter LLMs (Comma v0.1-1T and 2T) that attain competitive performance to models trained on unlicensed text under similar compute budgets.
findings: Largest collection of openly licensed text to date: an 8TB dataset drawn from 30 sources across diverse domains.
Trained two 7B-parameter models: Comma v0.1-1T (1 trillion tokens) and Comma v0.1-2T (2 trillion tokens).
Both models attain competitive performance with LLMs trained on unlicensed text at similar compute budgets, such as Llama 1 and Llama 2 7B.
Demonstrates that openly licensed data alone can be sufficient for competitive pretraining, challenging the assumption that unlicensed web text is required.

title: tau2-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
abstract: A benchmark that models customer-service agent interaction as a Dec-POMDP where both the agent and the user can take tool actions in a shared environment, with a compositional task generator, reliable user simulator, and a new telecom domain.
findings: Introduces dual-control (Dec-POMDP) evaluation where both agent and user use tools, unlike prior single-control benchmarks.
Adds a telecom domain with a compositional task generator producing diverse, verifiable tasks from atomic components.
Reports significant agent performance drops when shifting from no-user to dual-control settings.
Separates reasoning errors from coordination failures via a reliable user simulator.

title: Magistral
abstract: Technical report for Magistral, Mistral's first reasoning model, built with a from-scratch scalable RL pipeline relying solely on their own models and infrastructure rather than distilled traces from prior models.
findings: Ground-up RL approach: avoids RL traces distilled from existing reasoning models, relying solely on Mistral's own models and infrastructure.
Presents a simple method to force the reasoning language of the model.
Shows RL on text-only data maintains or improves multimodal understanding, instruction following, and function calling.
Magistral Medium is trained on Mistral Medium 3 with pure RL; Magistral Small (Apache 2.0) adds cold-start data distilled from Magistral Medium.
Demonstrates that pure RL training can reach strong reasoning while preserving most of the initial checkpoint's capabilities.

title: Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR
abstract: Shows that RLVR can elicit strong math reasoning in Qwen2.5-Math even with spurious rewards (random, format-only, or incorrect labels), raising questions about what RLVR actually optimizes and how model-dependent the effect is.
findings: On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, RLVR improves MATH-500 by 21.4% (random reward), 13.8% (format reward), 24.1% (incorrect label), 26.0% (1-shot RL), 27.1% (majority voting), vs 29.1% with ground-truth rewards.
Spurious rewards that work for Qwen often fail to help other model families like Llama3 or OLMo2.
'Code reasoning' (thinking in code without execution) becomes a distinctive Qwen2.5-Math behavior, rising from 65% to over 90% after RLVR even with spurious rewards.

title: Agent-RLVR: Training Software Engineering Agents via Guidance and Environment Rewards
abstract: Extends Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to complex agentic SWE settings by adding agent guidance that actively steers the agent toward successful trajectories, combined with environment validation rewards.
findings: On SWE-Bench Verified, Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct improves from 9.4% pass@1 (baseline) to 22.4% pass@1 with Agent-RLVR.
Adding test-time reward model training raises performance further to 27.8% pass@1.
Guidance mechanism provides informational cues that help agents recover from high-failure-rate trajectories.
Demonstrates RLVR can be made effective in multi-step agentic environments where vanilla RLVR degrades.

title: RoboArena: Distributed Real-World Evaluation of Generalist Robot Policies
abstract: A distributed, crowd-sourced methodology for evaluating generalist robot policies via double-blind pairwise comparisons across multiple institutions, aggregating preference feedback into reliable performance rankings.
findings: Conducts over 600 pairwise real-robot evaluations across diverse settings.
Tests 7 generalist policies across 7 academic institutions on the DROID platform.
Uses double-blind pairwise preference feedback rather than centralized standardized tasks.
Produces more accurate, scalable, and resilient rankings than conventional centralized evaluation.

title: RefineX: Learning to Refine Pre-training Data at Scale from Expert-Guided Programs
abstract: Proposes RefineX, a framework for large-scale refinement of pretraining data through programmatic editing. It distills expert-guided refinement results into edit-based deletion programs to train an efficient model that systematically improves corpus instances while preserving text diversity and naturalness.
findings: On the 750M model, RefineX yields 2.6%-7.2% average gains on lighteval tasks.
Achieves comparable performance using significantly fewer training tokens.
Outperforms models trained on raw, filtered, or alternatively refined data across diverse downstream tasks.
Beats prior approaches such as end-to-end generation and Prox-C.
Distills expert-guided refinement into edit-based deletion programs to preserve diversity and naturalness.

title: Training Long-Context, Multi-Turn Software Engineering Agents with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Applies modified DAPO-style RL to train long-context, multi-turn LLM agents for real-world software engineering tasks (issue resolution) without SFT, in interactive tool-using environments.
findings: Trains a multi-turn SWE agent with RL (a modified DAPO algorithm) directly, without an SFT warm-up stage.
On SWE-bench Verified, raises a Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct-based agent's resolve rate from 11% to 39% using RL alone.
Handles long-context, multi-turn interaction with a real code repository environment and tool use (editing, testing).
Demonstrates that purely RL-trained agents are competitive with much larger or SFT-pipelined open-weight agents on SWE tasks.
Addresses practical challenges of long-horizon, multi-turn credit assignment in agentic RL.

title: BeyondWeb: Lessons from Scaling Synthetic Data for Trillion-scale Pretraining
abstract: Introduces BeyondWeb, a synthetic data generation framework using targeted document rephrasing to produce diverse, relevant, information-dense synthetic pretraining data, addressing diminishing returns from simply scaling web-data quantity at trillion-token scale.
findings: Outperforms Cosmopedia by up to 5.1 percentage points and Nemotron-Synth by up to 2.6pp across 14 benchmarks.
Delivers up to 7.7x faster training than open web data and 2.7x faster than Nemotron-Synth.
A 3B model trained for 180B tokens on BeyondWeb outperforms an 8B model trained for the same token budget on Cosmopedia.
Emphasizes that best outcomes require jointly optimizing many factors rather than a single solution.
Trains 1B, 3B, and 8B models to validate scaling of synthetic data to trillion-token regimes.

title: Nemotron-CC-Math: A 133 Billion-Token-Scale High Quality Math Pretraining Dataset
abstract: Builds a high-quality math pretraining corpus from Common Crawl using layout-aware rendering with lynx plus a targeted LLM-based cleaning stage that recovers equations in MathJax, KaTeX, and MathML formats, preserving structure and standardizing notation to LaTeX. Releases Nemotron-CC-Math-3+ (133B tokens) and Nemotron-CC-Math-4+ (52B tokens).
findings: Nemotron-CC-Math-4+ (52B tokens) contains 5.5 times more tokens than FineMath-4+ and surpasses prior open math datasets including MegaMath, FineMath, and OpenWebMath.
Pretraining an 8B model yields +4.8 to +12.6 gains on MATH over strong baselines.
Yields +4.6 to +14.3 gains on MBPP+ over strong baselines.
Improves general reasoning on both MMLU and MMLU-Stem.
Uses layout-aware lynx rendering plus targeted LLM cleaning to recover equations across MathJax, KaTeX, and MathML and standardize to LaTeX.

title: Knowledge Collapse in LLMs: When Fluency Survives but Facts Fail under Recursive Synthetic Training
abstract: Examines how recursive training on synthetic data causes knowledge collapse, a distinct three-stage phenomenon where factual accuracy deteriorates while surface fluency persists, producing confidently-wrong outputs, and distinguishes this instruction-following/knowledge collapse from traditional distributional model collapse.
findings: Defines knowledge collapse as a three-stage phenomenon: factual accuracy deteriorates while surface fluency persists, creating confidently-wrong outputs.
Distinguishes knowledge/instruction-following collapse from traditional distributional model collapse.
Shows recursive synthetic training degrades facts faster than it degrades fluency.
Proposes domain-specific synthetic training as a mitigation strategy.

title: AgentArch: A Comprehensive Benchmark to Evaluate Agent Architectures in Enterprise
abstract: An enterprise-focused benchmark that systematically evaluates combinations of agent design dimensions (orchestration strategy, ReAct vs function calling, memory architecture, thinking-tool integration) across state-of-the-art LLMs.
findings: Evaluates 18 distinct agentic configurations across state-of-the-art LLMs over 4 critical design dimensions.
Reports maximum success rates of only 35.3% on complex tasks and 70.8% on simpler tasks.
Finds model-specific architectural preferences, challenging one-size-fits-all agent designs.
Highlights limited empirical understanding of how design dimensions interact in enterprise multi-agent systems.

title: FinSearchComp: Towards a Realistic, Expert-Level Evaluation of Financial Search and Reasoning
abstract: The first fully open-source agent benchmark for realistic, open-domain financial search and reasoning, with three task types mirroring analyst workflows and expert-annotated, multi-stage quality assurance.
findings: Contains 635 questions spanning global and Greater China markets across three tasks: Time-Sensitive Data Fetching, Simple Historical Lookup, and Complex Historical Investigation.
Engages 70 professional financial experts for annotation and QA; evaluates 21 models/products.
Grok 4 (web) tops the global subset approaching expert-level accuracy; DouBao (web) leads the Greater China subset.
Web search and financial plugins substantially improve results; model origin and tool selection significantly impact performance.

title: Synthetic Bootstrapped Pretraining
abstract: Proposes a pretraining procedure that first learns a model of relations between documents and then uses it to synthesize a vast new corpus for joint training, capturing inter-document correlations that standard token-level next-token prediction within single documents misses.
findings: Evaluated on 3B- and 6B-parameter models trained on up to 1T tokens from scratch in a compute-matched setup.
Delivers up to 60% of the performance improvement attainable by an oracle upper bound that has access to 20x more unique data.
Synthesized documents go beyond mere paraphrases, representing conceptual abstraction rather than surface rewriting.
Targets the data wall by extracting more signal from a fixed unique-data budget via inter-document relations.

title: Fleming-R1: Toward Expert-Level Medical Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: A medical reasoning model targeting verifiable clinical reasoning via a reasoning-oriented data strategy combining curated datasets with knowledge-graph synthesis, chain-of-thought cold start, and a two-stage RL framework using Group Relative Policy Optimization.
findings: The 7B variant surpasses significantly larger baselines on medical benchmarks.
The 32B model achieves near-parity with GPT-4o and consistently outperforms strong open-source alternatives.
Uses knowledge-graph-guided data synthesis to target identified reasoning failure modes.
Released publicly to support transparent, reproducible, auditable medical AI.

title: SWE-Bench Pro: Can AI Agents Solve Long-Horizon Software Engineering Tasks?
abstract: A contamination-resistant, human-verified benchmark of long-horizon software engineering tasks drawn from actively maintained repositories, spanning business applications, B2B services, and developer tools. Tasks often require patches across multiple files and substantial code modifications taking professional engineers hours to days.
findings: Contains 1,865 problems sourced from 41 actively maintained repositories.
Repositories split across a public set (11 repos), a held-out set (12 repos), and a commercial set of 18 proprietary repos.
Tasks are long-horizon, frequently requiring multi-file patches and substantial code changes.
All tasks go through a human augmentation and verification process to ensure descriptions and tests are well specified.

title: The Data-Quality Illusion: Rethinking Classifier-based Quality Filtering for LLM Pretraining (Removing Noise, not Finding Gold)
abstract: Analyzes Classifier-based Quality Filtering (CQF), the dominant method for filtering web-crawled pretraining data. Shows that training on CQF-selected data can outperform training directly on the high-quality target set, explaining this via the observation that CQF implicitly filters both the high- and low-quality datasets, and proposes an optimization-driven notion of data quality estimable through small-scale proxy experiments.
findings: Training on CQF-selected data can outperform training directly on the high-quality set, even when that set is sufficiently large.
CQF improves downstream task performance but does not necessarily improve language modeling on the high-quality dataset itself.
Explains the effect by showing CQF implicitly filters the high-quality dataset as well, acting more like noise removal than gold finding.
Proposes an optimization-driven notion of data quality reliably estimated via small-scale proxy experiments.

title: Demystifying Synthetic Data in LLM Pre-training: A Systematic Study of Scaling Laws, Benefits, and Pitfalls
abstract: A large-scale empirical study comparing natural web data against synthetic approaches (rephrased text and generated textbooks) for LLM pretraining, analyzing impact on performance, scaling, and compute efficiency across model sizes and data budgets.
findings: Pretraining on 1/3 rephrased synthetic data mixed with 2/3 natural web text can speed up reaching equivalent validation loss by 5-10x at larger data budgets.
Good ratios of synthetic data empirically converge to ~30% for rephrased synthetic data across model sizes and budgets.
Larger generator models do not necessarily yield better pretraining data than ~8B-parameter models.
Textbook-style synthetic data leads to notably higher loss on many downstream domains, especially at small data budgets.
Study spans over 1000 LLMs and over 100k GPU hours.

title: X-VLA: Soft-Prompted Transformer as Scalable Cross-Embodiment Vision-Language-Action Model
abstract: A scalable cross-embodiment vision-language-action model that uses learnable per-data-source soft-prompt embeddings with a flow-matching-based Transformer to handle heterogeneous robot data across embodiments, environments, and tasks.
findings: Introduces soft prompts (learnable embeddings per data source) with minimally added parameters to absorb cross-embodiment data heterogeneity.
X-VLA-0.9B simultaneously achieves SOTA performance across a sweep of benchmarks.
Validated across 6 simulations and 3 real-world robots.
Demonstrates flexible dexterity and quick adaptation across embodiments, environments, and tasks.

title: Escaping Model Collapse via Synthetic Data Verification: Near-term Improvements and Long-term Convergence
abstract: Investigates how to prevent model collapse from iteratively retraining generative models on self-generated synthetic data, showing both theoretically and empirically that incorporating external verification (human or from a superior model) prevents collapse, with verifier-guided retraining converging to the verifier's knowledge center.
findings: Shows incorporating external verification (human or a superior model) prevents model collapse in self-consuming training loops.
Theoretical analysis in linear regression: verifier-guided retraining produces initial gains but eventually converges to the verifier's knowledge center.
Validated across linear regression, VAEs on MNIST, and fine-tuning SmolLM2-135M on XSUM.
Frames verification as the key mechanism distinguishing safe self-improvement loops from degenerative ones.

title: Chem-R: Learning to Reason as a Chemist
abstract: A chemical reasoning model built via a three-phase framework (foundation training, protocol distillation with expert reasoning traces, and multi-task optimization) to emulate expert chemist reasoning across molecular and reaction tasks.
findings: Surpasses Gemini-2.5-Pro and DeepSeek-R1 by up to 32% on molecular tasks.
Outperforms leading models by up to 48% on reaction tasks.
Consistently exceeds existing chemical foundation models across molecular- and reaction-level benchmarks.
Uses distilled expert reasoning traces (protocol distillation) to instill structured chemical reasoning.

title: P1: Mastering Physics Olympiads with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: A family of open-source LLMs trained purely via reinforcement learning for Olympiad-level physics reasoning, achieving gold-medal performance at the International Physics Olympiad and strong cross-domain generalization.
findings: P1-235B-A22B (235B total / 22B active) is the first open-source model with Gold-medal performance at IPhO 2025.
Won 12 gold medals across 13 international/regional physics competitions in 2024/2025.
P1-30B-A3B (30B / 3B active) reaches silver-medal performance on IPhO 2025, surpassing most open-source models.
P1-235B-A22B combined with the PhysicsMinions agent framework achieves overall No.1 on IPhO 2025; models also generalize to math and coding.

title: SkyRL-Agent: Efficient RL Training for Multi-turn LLM Agent
abstract: A framework for efficient multi-turn LLM agent RL training featuring asynchronous dispatching, lightweight tool integration, and flexible backend interoperability, used to train a 32B SWE agent that generalizes across agentic tasks.
findings: Trains SA-SWE-32B (from Qwen3-32B), improving SWE-Bench Verified from 24.4% to 39.4% Pass@1.
Achieves over 2x cost reduction versus prior similar-performing models.
Pipeline dispatcher yields a 1.55x speedup over naive asynchronous batching.
SWE-only training generalizes to Terminal-Bench, BrowseComp-Plus, and WebArena.

title: Back to Basics: Revisiting Exploration in Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning via Generative Probabilities
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an indispensable paradigm for enhancing reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, standard policy optimization methods, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), often converge to low-entropy policies, leading to severe mode collapse and limited output diversity. We analyze this issue from the perspective of sampling probability dynamics, identifying that the standard objective disproportionately reinforces the highest-likelihood paths, thereby suppressing valid alternative reasoning chains. To address this, we propose a novel Advantage Re-weighting Mechanism (ARM) designed to equilibrate the confidence levels across all correct responses. By incorporating Prompt Perplexity and Answer Confidence into the advantage estimation, our method dynamically reshapes the reward signal to attenuate the gradient updates of over-confident reasoning paths, while redistributing probability mass toward under-explored correct solutions. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances generative diversity and response entropy while maintaining competitive accuracy, effectively achieving a superior trade-off between exploration and exploitation in reasoning tasks. Empirical results on Qwen2.5 and DeepSeek models across mathematical and coding benchmarks show that ProGRPO significantly mitigates entropy collapse. Specifically, on Qwen2.5-7B, our method outperforms GRPO by 5.7% in Pass@1 and, notably, by 13.9% in Pass@32, highlighting its superior capability in generating diverse correct reasoning paths.
findings: Identifies that GRPO over-reinforces highest-likelihood reasoning paths, causing entropy collapse and mode collapse.
Proposes an Advantage Re-weighting Mechanism (ARM) using prompt perplexity and answer confidence to redistribute reward toward under-explored correct solutions.
On Qwen2.5-7B, outperforms GRPO by 5.7% Pass@1 and 13.9% Pass@32 across math and coding benchmarks.
Improves generative diversity and response entropy while maintaining competitive accuracy on Qwen2.5 and DeepSeek models.

title: Not All Negative Samples Are Equal: LLMs Learn Better from Plausible Reasoning
abstract: Learning from negative samples holds great promise for improving Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning capability, yet existing methods treat all incorrect responses as equally informative, overlooking the crucial role of sample quality. To address this, we propose Plausible Negative Samples (PNS), a method that synthesizes high-quality negative samples exhibiting expected format and structural coherence while ultimately yielding incorrect answers. PNS trains a dedicated model via reverse reinforcement learning (RL) guided by a composite reward combining format compliance, accuracy inversion, reward model assessment, and chain-of-thought evaluation, generating responses nearly indistinguishable from correct solutions. We further validate PNS as a plug-and-play data source for preference optimization across three backbone models on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Results demonstrate that PNS consistently outperforms other negative sample synthesis methods, achieving an average improvement of 2.03% over RL-trained models.
findings: Argues incorrect responses are not equally informative; synthesizes high-quality 'plausible' negatives that look correct in format and structure but reach wrong answers.
Trains a dedicated generator via reverse RL using a composite reward (format compliance, accuracy inversion, reward-model score, CoT evaluation).
Used as plug-and-play preference-optimization data across three backbone models and seven math reasoning benchmarks.
Consistently beats other negative-sample synthesis methods, averaging +2.03% over RL-trained baselines.

title: Continual Pretraining on Encrypted Synthetic Data for Privacy-Preserving LLMs
abstract: Preserving privacy in sensitive data while pretraining large language models on small, domain-specific corpora presents a significant challenge. In this work, we take an exploratory step toward privacy-preserving continual pretraining by proposing an entity-based framework that synthesizes encrypted training data to protect personally identifiable information (PII). Our approach constructs a weighted entity graph to guide data synthesis and applies deterministic encryption to PII entities, enabling LLMs to encode new knowledge through continual pretraining while granting authorized access to sensitive data through decryption keys. Our results on limited-scale datasets demonstrate that our pretrained models outperform base models and ensure PII security, while exhibiting a modest performance gap compared to models trained on unencrypted synthetic data. We further show that increasing the number of entities and leveraging graph-based synthesis improves model performance, and that encrypted models retain instruction-following capabilities with long retrieved contexts. We discuss the security implications and limitations of deterministic encryption, positioning this work as an initial investigation into the design space of encrypted data pretraining for privacy-preserving LLMs.
findings: Proposes an entity-based framework that synthesizes encrypted training data, deterministically encrypting PII entities while guided by a weighted entity graph.
Pretrained models outperform base models and preserve PII security, with only a modest gap versus unencrypted synthetic data.
More entities and graph-based synthesis improve downstream performance.
Encrypted models retain instruction-following ability even with long retrieved contexts.

title: OPUS: Towards Efficient and Principled Data Selection in Large Language Model Pre-training in Every Iteration
abstract: As high-quality public text approaches exhaustion, a phenomenon known as the Data Wall, pre-training is shifting from more tokens to better tokens. However, existing methods either rely on heuristic static filters that ignore training dynamics, or use dynamic yet optimizer-agnostic criteria based on raw gradients. We propose OPUS (Optimizer-induced Projected Utility Selection), a dynamic data selection framework that defines utility in the optimizer-induced update space. OPUS scores candidates by projecting their effective updates, shaped by modern optimizers, onto a target direction derived from a stable, in-distribution proxy. To ensure scalability, we employ Ghost technique with CountSketch for computational efficiency, and Boltzmann sampling for data diversity, incurring only 4.7% additional compute overhead. OPUS achieves remarkable results across diverse corpora, quality tiers, optimizers, and model scales. In pre-training of GPT-2 Large/XL on FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu with 30B tokens, OPUS outperforms industrial-level baselines and even full 200B-token training. Moreover, when combined with industrial-level static filters, OPUS further improves pre-training efficiency, even with lower-quality data. Furthermore, in continued pre-training of Qwen3-8B-Base on SciencePedia, OPUS achieves superior performance using only 0.5B tokens compared to full training with 3B tokens, demonstrating significant data efficiency gains in specialized domains.
findings: Frames the 'Data Wall' as a shift from more tokens to better tokens; defines data utility in the optimizer-induced update space rather than raw gradients.
Adds only 4.7% compute overhead via Ghost/CountSketch projection plus Boltzmann sampling for diversity.
Pre-training GPT-2 Large/XL on FineWeb/FineWeb-Edu with 30B tokens, OPUS beats industrial baselines and even full 200B-token training.
In continued pre-training of Qwen3-8B-Base on SciencePedia, OPUS matches/exceeds 3B-token full training using only 0.5B tokens.

title: DataFlex: A Unified Framework for Data-Centric Dynamic Training of Large Language Models
abstract: Data-centric training has emerged as a promising direction for improving large language models (LLMs) by optimizing not only model parameters but also the selection, composition, and weighting of training data during optimization. However, existing approaches to data selection, data mixture optimization, and data reweighting are often developed in isolated codebases with inconsistent interfaces, hindering reproducibility, fair comparison, and practical integration. In this paper, we present DataFlex, a unified data-centric dynamic training framework built upon LLaMA-Factory. DataFlex supports three major paradigms of dynamic data optimization: sample selection, domain mixture adjustment, and sample reweighting, while remaining fully compatible with the original training workflow. It provides extensible trainer abstractions and modular components, enabling a drop-in replacement for standard LLM training, and unifies key model-dependent operations such as embedding extraction, inference, and gradient computation, with support for large-scale settings including DeepSpeed ZeRO-3. We conduct comprehensive experiments across multiple data-centric methods. Dynamic data selection consistently outperforms static full-data training on MMLU across both Mistral-7B and Llama-3.2-3B. For data mixture, DoReMi and ODM improve both MMLU accuracy and corpus-level perplexity over default proportions when pretraining Qwen2.5-1.5B on SlimPajama at 6B and 30B token scales. DataFlex also achieves consistent runtime improvements over original implementations. These results demonstrate that DataFlex provides an effective, efficient, and reproducible infrastructure for data-centric dynamic training of LLMs.
findings: Unifies sample selection, domain-mixture adjustment, and sample reweighting in one LLaMA-Factory-based framework (with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 support).
Dynamic data selection consistently beats static full-data training on MMLU for Mistral-7B and Llama-3.2-3B.
DoReMi and ODM mixture methods improve MMLU accuracy and corpus perplexity pretraining Qwen2.5-1.5B on SlimPajama at 6B and 30B tokens.
Delivers consistent runtime improvements over original method implementations.

title: CHIMERA: Compact Synthetic Data for Generalizable LLM Reasoning
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently exhibited remarkable reasoning capabilities, largely enabled by supervised fine-tuning (SFT)- and reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training on high-quality reasoning data. However, reproducing and extending these capabilities in open and scalable settings is hindered by three fundamental data-centric challenges: (1) the cold-start problem, arising from the lack of seed datasets with detailed, long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) trajectories needed to initialize reasoning policies; (2) limited domain coverage, as most existing open-source reasoning datasets are concentrated in mathematics, with limited coverage of broader scientific disciplines; and (3) the annotation bottleneck, where the difficulty of frontier-level reasoning tasks makes reliable human annotation prohibitively expensive or infeasible. To address these challenges, we introduce CHIMERA, a compact synthetic reasoning dataset comprising 9K samples for generalizable cross-domain reasoning. CHIMERA is constructed with three key properties: (1) it provides rich, long CoT reasoning trajectories synthesized by state-of-the-art reasoning models; (2) it has broad and structured coverage, spanning 8 major scientific disciplines and over 1K fine-grained topics organized via a model-generated hierarchical taxonomy; and (3) it employs a fully automated, scalable evaluation pipeline that uses strong reasoning models to cross-validate both problem validity and answer correctness. We use CHIMERA to post-train a 4B Qwen3 model. Despite the dataset's modest size, the resulting model achieves strong performance on a suite of challenging reasoning benchmarks, including GPQA-Diamond, AIME 24/25/26, HMMT 25, and Humanity's Last Exam, approaching or matching the reasoning performance of substantially larger models such as DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-235B.
findings: A compact 9K-sample synthetic reasoning dataset with long CoT trajectories spanning 8 scientific disciplines and 1K+ fine-grained topics via a model-generated taxonomy.
Uses a fully automated pipeline where strong reasoning models cross-validate both problem validity and answer correctness.
Post-training a 4B Qwen3 model on CHIMERA approaches or matches far larger models (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-235B).
Strong results on GPQA-Diamond, AIME 24/25/26, HMMT 25, and Humanity's Last Exam despite the dataset's small size.

title: LiveClin: A Live Clinical Benchmark without Leakage
abstract: The reliability of medical LLM evaluation is critically undermined by data contamination and knowledge obsolescence, leading to inflated scores on static benchmarks. To address these challenges, we introduce LiveClin, a live benchmark designed for approximating real-world clinical practice. Built from contemporary, peer-reviewed case reports and updated biannually, LiveClin ensures clinical currency and resists data contamination. Using a verified AI-human workflow involving 239 physicians, we transform authentic patient cases into complex, multimodal evaluation scenarios that span the entire clinical pathway. The benchmark currently comprises 1,407 case reports and 6,605 questions. Our evaluation of 26 models on LiveClin reveals the profound difficulty of these real-world scenarios, with the top-performing model achieving a Case Accuracy of just 35.7%. In benchmarking against human experts, Chief Physicians achieved the highest accuracy, followed closely by Attending Physicians, with both surpassing most models. LiveClin thus provides a continuously evolving, clinically grounded framework to guide the development of medical LLMs towards closing this gap and achieving greater reliability and real-world utility.
findings: Live, biannually-updated clinical benchmark built from contemporary peer-reviewed case reports to resist contamination and obsolescence.
Uses an AI-human workflow with 239 physicians; 1,407 case reports and 6,605 multimodal questions spanning the full clinical pathway.
Across 26 models, the top model reaches only 35.7% Case Accuracy, exposing the difficulty of real-world clinical scenarios.
Chief and Attending Physicians outperform most models, quantifying the human-model gap in clinical practice.

title: PLawBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs in Real-World Legal Practice
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to legal domain-specific tasks, evaluating their ability to perform legal work in real-world settings has become essential. However, existing legal benchmarks rely on simplified and highly standardized tasks, failing to capture the ambiguity, complexity, and reasoning demands of real legal practice. Moreover, prior evaluations often adopt coarse, single-dimensional metrics and do not explicitly assess fine-grained legal reasoning. To address these limitations, we introduce PLawBench, a Practical Law Benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs in realistic legal practice scenarios. Grounded in real-world legal workflows, PLawBench models the core processes of legal practitioners through three task categories: public legal consultation, practical case analysis, and legal document generation. These tasks assess a model's ability to identify legal issues and key facts, perform structured legal reasoning, and generate legally coherent documents. PLawBench comprises 850 questions across 13 practical legal scenarios, with each question accompanied by expert-designed evaluation rubrics, resulting in approximately 12,500 rubric items for fine-grained assessment. Using an LLM-based evaluator aligned with human expert judgments, we evaluate 10 state-of-the-art LLMs. Experimental results show that none achieves strong performance on PLawBench, revealing substantial limitations in the fine-grained legal reasoning capabilities of current LLMs and highlighting important directions for future evaluation and development of legal LLMs.
findings: Rubric-based legal benchmark grounded in real practitioner workflows: legal consultation, case analysis, and document generation.
850 questions across 13 practical scenarios with ~12,500 expert-designed rubric items for fine-grained scoring.
Uses an LLM-based evaluator aligned to human expert judgments to grade 10 state-of-the-art LLMs.
No current model performs strongly, exposing substantial limits in fine-grained legal reasoning.

title: FinTradeBench: A Financial Reasoning Benchmark for LLMs
abstract: Real-world financial decision-making is a challenging problem that requires reasoning over heterogeneous signals, including company fundamentals derived from regulatory filings and trading signals computed from price dynamics. Recently, with advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), financial analysts have begun to use them for financial decision-making tasks. However, existing financial question-answering benchmarks for testing these models primarily focus on company balance sheet data and rarely evaluate reasoning about how company stocks trade in the market or their interactions with fundamentals. To leverage the strengths of both approaches, we introduce FinTradeBench, a benchmark for evaluating financial reasoning that integrates company fundamentals and trading signals. FinTradeBench contains 1,400 questions grounded in NASDAQ-100 companies over a ten-year historical window. The benchmark is organized into three reasoning categories: fundamentals-focused, trading-signal-focused, and hybrid questions requiring cross-signal reasoning. To ensure reliability at scale, we adopt a calibration-then-scaling framework that combines expert seed questions, multi-model response generation, intra-model self-filtering, numerical auditing, and human-LLM judge alignment. We evaluate 14 LLMs under zero-shot prompting and retrieval-augmented settings and witness a clear performance gap. Retrieval substantially improves reasoning over textual fundamentals, but provides limited benefit for trading-signal reasoning. These findings highlight fundamental challenges in the numerical and time-series reasoning for current LLMs and motivate future research in financial intelligence.
findings: Financial reasoning benchmark integrating company fundamentals (regulatory filings) and market trading signals.
1,400 questions grounded in NASDAQ-100 companies over a ten-year window, split into fundamentals-focused, trading-signal-focused, and hybrid categories.
Built via a calibration-then-scaling pipeline (expert seeds, multi-model generation, self-filtering, numerical auditing, human-LLM judge alignment).
Across 14 LLMs, retrieval helps reasoning over textual fundamentals but barely helps trading-signal reasoning, exposing weak numerical/time-series reasoning.

title: EvoCodeBench: A Human-Performance Benchmark for Self-Evolving LLM-Driven Coding Systems
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance in programming tasks, LLM-driven coding systems have evolved from one-shot code generation into complex systems capable of iterative improvement during inference. However, existing code benchmarks primarily emphasize static correctness and implicitly assume fixed model capability during inference. As a result, they do not capture inference-time self-evolution, such as whether accuracy and efficiency improve as an agent iteratively refines its solutions. They also provide limited accounting of resource costs and rarely calibrate model performance against that of human programmers. Moreover, many benchmarks are dominated by high-resource languages, leaving cross-language robustness and long-tail language stability underexplored. Therefore, we present EvoCodeBench, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving LLM-driven coding systems across programming languages with direct comparison to human performance. EvoCodeBench tracks performance dynamics, measuring solution correctness alongside efficiency metrics such as solving time, memory consumption, and improvement algorithmic design over repeated problem-solving attempts. To ground evaluation in a human-centered reference frame, we directly compare model performance with that of human programmers on the same tasks, enabling relative performance assessment within the human ability distribution. Furthermore, EvoCodeBench supports multiple programming languages, enabling systematic cross-language and long-tail stability analyses under a unified protocol. Our results demonstrate that self-evolving systems exhibit measurable gains in efficiency over time, and that human-relative and multi-language analyses provide insights unavailable through accuracy alone. EvoCodeBench establishes a foundation for evaluating coding intelligence in evolving LLM-driven systems.
findings: Benchmark for self-evolving coding systems that captures inference-time self-improvement, not just static one-shot correctness.
Tracks correctness plus efficiency metrics (solving time, memory, algorithmic design) over repeated refinement attempts.
Directly calibrates model performance against human programmers on identical tasks for human-relative assessment.
Multi-language design enables cross-language and long-tail stability analysis; self-evolving systems show measurable efficiency gains over time.

title: SWE-MiniSandbox: Container-Free Reinforcement Learning for Building Software Engineering Agents
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a key paradigm for training software engineering (SWE) agents, but existing pipelines typically rely on per-task containers for isolation. At scale, pre-built container images incur substantial storage overhead, slow environment setup, and require container-management privileges. We propose SWE-MiniSandbox, a lightweight, container-free method that enables scalable RL training of SWE agents without sacrificing isolation. Instead of relying on per-instance containers, SWE-MiniSandbox executes each task in an isolated workspace backed by kernel-level mechanisms, substantially reducing system overhead. It leverages lightweight environment pre-caching techniques to eliminate the need for bulky container images. As a result, our approach lowers disk usage to approximately 5% of that required by container-based pipelines and reduces environment preparation time to about 25% of the container baseline. Empirical results demonstrate that SWE-MiniSandbox achieves evaluation performance comparable to standard container-based pipelines. By removing the dependency on heavy container infrastructure, SWE-MiniSandbox offers a practical and accessible foundation for scaling RL-based SWE agents, particularly in resource-constrained research environments.
findings: Container-free RL training environment for software-engineering agents, using kernel-level isolation instead of per-task containers.
Lowers disk usage to ~5% and environment preparation time to ~25% of container-based pipelines.
Achieves evaluation performance comparable to standard container-based RL pipelines.
Lightweight environment pre-caching removes the need for bulky per-instance container images, easing RL scaling in resource-constrained settings.

title: ReplicatorBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Replicability in Social and Behavioral Sciences
abstract: The literature has witnessed an emerging interest in AI agents for automated assessment of scientific papers. Existing benchmarks focus primarily on the computational aspect of this task, testing agents' ability to reproduce or replicate research outcomes when having access to the code and data. This setting, while foundational, (1) fails to capture the inconsistent availability of new data for replication as opposed to reproduction, and (2) lacks ground-truth diversity by focusing only on reproducible papers, thereby failing to evaluate an agent's ability to identify non-replicable research. Furthermore, most benchmarks only evaluate outcomes rather than the replication process. In response, we introduce ReplicatorBench, an end-to-end benchmark, including human-verified replicable and non-replicable research claims in social and behavioral sciences for evaluating AI agents in research replication across three stages: (1) extraction and retrieval of replication data; (2) design and execution of computational experiments; and (3) interpretation of results, allowing a test of AI agents' capability to mimic the activities of human replicators in real world. To set a baseline of AI agents' capability, we develop ReplicatorAgent, an agentic framework equipped with necessary tools, like web search and iterative interaction with sandboxed environments, to accomplish tasks in ReplicatorBench. We evaluate ReplicatorAgent across four underlying large language models (LLMs), as well as different design choices of programming language and levels of code access. Our findings reveal that while current LLM agents are capable of effectively designing and executing computational experiments, they struggle with retrieving resources, such as new data, necessary to replicate a claim.
findings: End-to-end benchmark for research replication in social and behavioral sciences, including both replicable and non-replicable human-verified claims.
Evaluates three stages: replication-data extraction/retrieval, experiment design/execution, and results interpretation.
Provides ReplicatorAgent (web search + sandboxed execution) as a baseline across four underlying LLMs.
Agents can design and execute experiments well but struggle to retrieve the new data/resources needed to replicate a claim.

title: Group Sequence Policy Optimization
authors: Chujie Zheng et al. (Qwen Team, Alibaba)
abstract: This paper introduces Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), our stable, efficient, and performant reinforcement learning algorithm for training large language models. Unlike previous algorithms that adopt token-level importance ratios, GSPO defines the importance ratio based on sequence likelihood and performs sequence-level clipping, rewarding, and optimization. We demonstrate that GSPO achieves superior training efficiency and performance compared to the GRPO algorithm, notably stabilizes Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) RL training, and has the potential for simplifying the design of RL infrastructure. These merits of GSPO have contributed to the remarkable improvements in the latest Qwen3 models.
findings: GSPO replaces GRPO's token-level importance ratio with a sequence-level importance ratio, performing sequence-level clipping, rewarding, and optimization to align the optimization unit with the reward unit.
Achieves superior training efficiency and performance over GRPO, and notably stabilizes Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) RL training where token-level ratios are ill-posed.
Directly contributed to the improvements in the production Qwen3 models and can simplify RL infrastructure design.

title: Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence
abstract: We introduce Kimi K2, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language model with 32 billion activated parameters and 1 trillion total parameters. We propose the MuonClip optimizer, which improves upon Muon with a novel QK-clip technique to address training instability while enjoying the advanced token efficiency of Muon. Based on MuonClip, K2 was pre-trained on 15.5 trillion tokens with zero loss spike. During post-training, K2 undergoes a multi-stage post-training process, highlighted by a large-scale agentic data synthesis pipeline and a joint reinforcement learning (RL) stage, where the model improves its capabilities through interactions with real and synthetic environments. Kimi K2 achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source non-thinking models, with strengths in agentic capabilities. Notably, K2 obtains 66.1 on Tau2-Bench, 76.5 on ACEBench (En), 65.8 on SWE-Bench Verified, and 47.3 on SWE-Bench Multilingual -- surpassing most open and closed-sourced baselines in non-thinking settings. It also exhibits strong capabilities in coding, mathematics, and reasoning tasks, with a score of 53.7 on LiveCodeBench v6, 49.5 on AIME 2025, 75.1 on GPQA-Diamond, and 27.1 on OJBench, all without extended thinking.
findings: 1T-parameter MoE (32B active) pre-trained on 15.5T tokens with zero loss spikes using the new MuonClip optimizer (Muon + QK-clip for stability).

Post-training combines a large-scale agentic-data synthesis pipeline with a joint RL stage where the model learns via interaction with real and synthetic environments, plus a self-critique rubric reward extending RLVR to open-ended tasks.
SOTA among open non-thinking models: 65.8 SWE-bench Verified, 66.1 Tau2-Bench, 53.7 LiveCodeBench v6, 49.5 AIME 2025, 75.1 GPQA-Diamond.

title: In-the-Flow Agentic System Optimization for Effective Planning and Tool Use
abstract: Outcome-driven reinforcement learning has advanced reasoning in large language models (LLMs), but prevailing tool-augmented approaches train a single, monolithic policy that interleaves thoughts and tool calls under full context; this scales poorly with long horizons and diverse tools and generalizes weakly to new scenarios. Agentic systems offer a promising alternative by decomposing work across specialized modules, yet most remain training-free or rely on offline training decoupled from the live dynamics of multi-turn interaction. We introduce AgentFlow, a trainable, in-the-flow agentic framework that coordinates four modules (planner, executor, verifier, generator) through an evolving memory and directly optimizes its planner inside the multi-turn loop. To train on-policy in live environments, we propose Flow-based Group Refined Policy Optimization (Flow-GRPO), which tackles long-horizon, sparse-reward credit assignment by converting multi-turn optimization into a sequence of tractable single-turn policy updates. It broadcasts a single, verifiable trajectory-level outcome to every turn to align local planner decisions with global success and stabilizes learning with group-normalized advantages. Across ten benchmarks, AgentFlow with a 7B-scale backbone outperforms top-performing baselines with average accuracy gains of 14.9% on search, 14.0% on agentic, 14.5% on mathematical, and 4.1% on scientific tasks, even surpassing larger proprietary models like GPT-4o. Further analyses confirm the benefits of in-the-flow optimization, showing improved planning, enhanced tool-calling reliability, and positive scaling with model size and reasoning turns.
findings: AgentFlow trains the planner module on-policy inside a live multi-turn agentic loop (planner/executor/verifier/generator with evolving memory), rather than as a monolithic context-stuffed policy.

Flow-GRPO converts long-horizon sparse-reward multi-turn optimization into tractable single-turn updates by broadcasting one verifiable trajectory-level outcome to every turn, with group-normalized advantages for stability.
A 7B-backbone AgentFlow beats strong baselines across 10 benchmarks (search +14.9%, agentic +14.0%, math +14.5%, scientific +4.1%) and surpasses larger proprietary models including GPT-4o.

title: The Art of Scaling Reinforcement Learning Compute for LLMs
authors: Devvrit Khatri, Lovish Madaan et al. (incl. Rishabh Agarwal)
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central to training large language models (LLMs), yet the field lacks predictive scaling methodologies comparable to those established for pre-training. Despite rapidly rising compute budgets, there is no principled understanding of how to evaluate algorithmic improvements for scaling RL compute. We present the first large-scale systematic study, amounting to more than 400,000 GPU-hours, that defines a principled framework for analyzing and predicting RL scaling in LLMs. We fit sigmoidal compute-performance curves for RL training and ablate a wide range of common design choices to analyze their effects on asymptotic performance and compute efficiency. We observe: (1) Not all recipes yield similar asymptotic performance, (2) Details such as loss aggregation, normalization, curriculum, and off-policy algorithm primarily modulate compute efficiency without materially shifting the asymptote, and (3) Stable, scalable recipes follow predictable scaling trajectories, enabling extrapolation from smaller-scale runs. Combining these insights, we propose a best-practice recipe, ScaleRL, and demonstrate its effectiveness by successfully scaling and predicting validation performance on a single RL run scaled up to 100,000 GPU-hours. Our work provides both a scientific framework for analyzing scaling in RL and a practical recipe that brings RL training closer to the predictability long achieved in pre-training.
findings: First large-scale (>400,000 GPU-hours) study fitting sigmoidal compute-performance curves for RL, enabling prediction of asymptotic performance from small-scale runs.
Many design choices (loss aggregation, normalization, curriculum, off-policy algorithm) mainly modulate compute efficiency but do not shift the asymptote; recipe choice does change the asymptote.
Proposes the ScaleRL best-practice recipe and validates it on a single run scaled to 100,000 GPU-hours, matching the extrapolated curve.

title: DeepSeek-V3.2: Pushing the Frontier of Open Large Language Models
abstract: We introduce DeepSeek-V3.2, a model that harmonizes high computational efficiency with superior reasoning and agent performance. The key technical breakthroughs of DeepSeek-V3.2 are as follows: (1) DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA): We introduce DSA, an efficient attention mechanism that substantially reduces computational complexity while preserving model performance in long-context scenarios. (2) Scalable Reinforcement Learning Framework: By implementing a robust reinforcement learning protocol and scaling post-training compute, DeepSeek-V3.2 performs comparably to GPT-5. Notably, our high-compute variant, DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale, surpasses GPT-5 and exhibits reasoning proficiency on par with Gemini-3.0-Pro, achieving gold-medal performance in both the 2025 International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) and the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI). (3) Large-Scale Agentic Task Synthesis Pipeline: To integrate reasoning into tool-use scenarios, we developed a novel synthesis pipeline that systematically generates training data at scale. This methodology facilitates scalable agentic post-training, yielding substantial improvements in generalization and instruction-following robustness within complex, interactive environments.
findings: Scaling post-training RL compute brings DeepSeek-V3.2 to parity with GPT-5; the high-compute DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale variant surpasses GPT-5 and matches Gemini-3.0-Pro, winning gold at IMO 2025 and IOI 2025.
A Large-Scale Agentic Task Synthesis Pipeline generates tool-use training data at scale, yielding substantial gains in generalization and instruction-following robustness in interactive environments.
DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) cuts computational complexity while preserving long-context performance, making the scaled RL post-training tractable.

title: Native Sparse Attention: Hardware-Aligned and Natively Trainable Sparse Attention
abstract: Long-context modeling is crucial for next-generation language models, yet the high computational cost of standard attention mechanisms poses significant computational challenges. Sparse attention offers a promising direction for improving efficiency while maintaining model capabilities. We present NSA, a Natively trainable Sparse Attention mechanism that integrates algorithmic innovations with hardware-aligned optimizations to achieve efficient long-context modeling. NSA employs a dynamic hierarchical sparse strategy, combining coarse-grained token compression with fine-grained token selection to preserve both global context awareness and local precision. Our approach advances sparse attention design with two key innovations: (1) We achieve substantial speedups through arithmetic intensity-balanced algorithm design, with implementation optimizations for modern hardware. (2) We enable end-to-end training, reducing pretraining computation without sacrificing model performance. As shown in Figure 1, experiments show the model pretrained with NSA maintains or exceeds Full Attention models across general benchmarks, long-context tasks, and instruction-based reasoning. Meanwhile, NSA achieves substantial speedups over Full Attention on 64k-length sequences across decoding, forward propagation, and backward propagation, validating its efficiency throughout the model lifecycle.
findings: Hierarchical sparse design combines coarse-grained token compression, fine-grained token selection, and sliding local windows; natively trainable end-to-end (not a post-hoc inference trick).
On 64k-length sequences, achieves up to 11.6x speedup in decoding, 9.0x in forward propagation, and 6.0x in backward propagation vs Full Attention.
Pretrained NSA model matches or exceeds Full Attention models on general benchmarks, long-context tasks, and instruction-based reasoning.
Achieves perfect retrieval accuracy across all positions in 64k-context needle-in-a-haystack tests.

title: Muon is Scalable for LLM Training
abstract: Recently, the Muon optimizer based on matrix orthogonalization has demonstrated strong results in training small-scale language models, but the scalability to larger models has not been proven. We identify two crucial techniques for scaling up Muon: (1) adding weight decay and (2) carefully adjusting the per-parameter update scale. These techniques allow Muon to work out-of-the-box on large-scale training without the need of hyper-parameter tuning. Scaling law experiments indicate that Muon achieves ~2x computational efficiency compared to AdamW with compute optimal training. Based on these improvements, we introduce Moonlight, a 3B/16B-parameter Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) model trained with 5.7T tokens using Muon. Our model improves the current Pareto frontier, achieving better performance with much fewer training FLOPs compared to prior models. We open-source our distributed Muon implementation that is memory optimal and communication efficient. We also release the pretrained, instruction-tuned, and intermediate checkpoints to support future research.
findings: Two techniques make Muon scale out-of-the-box without hyperparameter tuning: (1) adding weight decay and (2) carefully adjusting the per-parameter update scale.
Scaling-law experiments show ~2x computational efficiency vs AdamW at compute-optimal training.
Introduces Moonlight, a 3B/16B-active MoE trained on 5.7T tokens with Muon, improving the performance/FLOPs Pareto frontier.
Open-sources a memory-optimal, communication-efficient distributed Muon implementation plus pretrained/instruction/intermediate checkpoints.

title: MiniMax-01: Scaling Foundation Models with Lightning Attention
abstract: We introduce MiniMax-01 series, including MiniMax-Text-01 and MiniMax-VL-01, which are comparable to top-tier models while offering superior capabilities in processing longer contexts. The core lies in lightning attention and its efficient scaling.
